actual_support_paragraphs: 1.1 Set $E(x,t)=E_q(x)$ time-independently and put $B=0$, $J=0$. Since $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$, the other three equations listed in [A1] hold with both sides zero. This is a distributional vacuum Maxwell solution with the stated stationary point source. [A1, F1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 The shell in [F2] with outer radius $R/2$ lies inside $B_R(x_0)$. This lower bound is unbounded as $\delta\downarrow0$ because $q^2/\varepsilon_0>0$; thus each ball around $x_0$ has infinite ordinary electric energy and $u_E\notin L^1$ near the charge. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], a field with nonintegrable ordinary quadratic energy is outside the finite-energy boundary model, even though step 1.1 supplies its distributional Maxwell identities. This contradicts the refuted claim and proves the counterexample. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, contradiction] ∎

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
For complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ at frequency
$\omega$, the real-field encoding assigns the maps
$\mathbf E,\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right),\qquad \mathbf B(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf b e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\right).$$
In the SI field interpretation, $\mathbf e$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$
and $\mathbf b$ has units tesla. The candidate is an **exact
source-free vacuum plane-wave mode** precisely when these real fields are
jointly $C^1$ and satisfy, pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$,
$$\operatorname{div}\mathbf E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf B=c^{-2}\partial_t\mathbf E,$$
the zero-source specialization of the adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch.
The longitudinal electric coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

1.2 By [F3], every scalar spectral measure of $H_0$ is absolutely continuous, so $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)=I$. Thus the projection in [F5] drops out. Since $HJ=JH_0$ and both generators are bounded, direct differentiation gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}) =i e^{itH}(HJ-JH_0)e^{-itH_0}=0$. Thus the approximants are constant and both strong limits exist with $\Omega_\pm f=(f,0)$. Their norm equals $\|f\|$, so they are isometries. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

1.3 By [F3], every vector $f\oplus g\in\mathcal H$ has scalar spectral measure $B\longmapsto\int_{B\cap(0,1)}(|f(x)|^2+|g(x)|^2)\,dx$, which is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Therefore $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The wave-operator range is $\mathcal H_0\oplus\{0\}$, which is a proper subspace of $\mathcal H$ because the constant function $1\in L^2((0,1))$ has norm one, so $0\oplus1$ is a nonzero vector outside the range. Hence the wave operators are isometric but not complete, refuting the statement. [F1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

supporting_current_arguments.exact_current_excerpt:
For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$.

Equip $\mathbb R^m$ with the dot product $c^\mathsf Tb=\sum_{a=1}^m c_ab_a$. Here $S^*:\mathsf H_d\to\mathbb R^m$ denotes the adjoint relative to this dot product and the displayed trace pairing: it is characterized by $c^\mathsf T(S^*X)=\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}$ for every $c\in\mathbb R^m$ and $X\in\mathsf H_d$. The following lemma proves that the trace pairing is an inner product and that this adjoint exists as a well-defined linear map; it also establishes that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

supporting_current_arguments.exact_current_excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$, $p\in[0,1]$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n:\Omega\to\{0,1\}$ be measurable on a probability space with
$$\mathbb P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n)=\prod_{k=1}^n b_p(x_k)\quad\text{for every }(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n.$$
Here $b_p(1)=p$ and $b_p(0)=1-p$, including $p=0$ and $p=1$. Thus the variables have the stated independent Bernoulli product law. For their frequency $f=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and every $t>0$,
$$
\mathbb P(|f-p|\ge t)\le2e^{-2nt^2}.
$$
No axiom of choice is assumed.

1.1 Summing the product law [A1] over the other $n-1$ coordinates gives $\mathbb P(X_k=1)=p\prod_{j\ne k}(p+(1-p))=p$, so $\mathbb E X_k=p$. Put $S=\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-p)$. By [F1], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(X_k-p)}\le e^{\lambda^2/8}$ for every real $\lambda$. Expanding the finite expectation over $\{0,1\}^n$ and using [A1] factors it into the product of these $n$ expectations. Hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S}\le e^{n\lambda^2/8}$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $\lambda>0$, $S\ge nt$ implies $e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda nt}$. For any nonnegative $W$ and $c>0$, $W\ge c\,\mathbf1_{\{W\ge c\}}$, so $\mathbb P(W\ge c)\le\mathbb EW/c$. Apply this to $W=e^{\lambda S}$ and then step 1.1 to get $\mathbb P(f-p\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda nt+n\lambda^2/8}$. Setting $\lambda=4t$ gives $e^{-2nt^2}$. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the same argument to $-S$, using step 1.1 at $-4t$; it gives $\mathbb P(p-f\ge t)\le e^{-2nt^2}$. The union bound follows from $\mathbf1_{A\cup B}\le\mathbf1_A+\mathbf1_B$, so adding the two tails proves the claim. If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)D_a.
$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

2.1 Regard the real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $G$ as a complex Hermitian matrix and apply [F3]. Its eigenvalues are real. If $z=x+iy$ is in the complex eigenspace for a real eigenvalue $\lambda$, then realness of $G$ gives $Gx=\lambda x$ and $Gy=\lambda y$; thus that eigenspace is the complexification of its real eigenspace. Real eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, since $Gu=\lambda u$, $Gv=\mu v$, and symmetry give $(\lambda-\mu)u^{\mathsf T}v=0$. The real eigenspaces form a direct sum of dimension $m$: their complexifications are the orthogonal complex eigenspaces, which span $\mathbb C^m$ by [F3]. Each eigenvalue is nonnegative because, for a nonzero real eigenvector $x$ with $Gx=\lambda x$, $\lambda\|x\|_2^2=x^\mathsf T Gx\ge0$. In each real eigenspace, take a finite basis $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ and set $u_1=v_1/\|v_1\|_2$ and $u_j=(v_j-\sum_{i<j}(v_j^\mathsf T u_i)u_i)/\|v_j-\sum_{i<j}(v_j^\mathsf T u_i)u_i\|_2$ for $2\le j\le k$; basis independence makes every denominator nonzero, and these vectors form a real orthonormal basis. These bases give a real spectral resolution $G=\sum_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda P_\lambda$ with real orthogonal projections whose sum is $I$. Put $H_0=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Orthogonality gives $GH_0G=G$, $H_0GH_0=H_0$, and $GH_0=H_0G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda$, which are self-adjoint. Thus $H_0$ satisfies the four Penrose equations [F4], and uniqueness in [F5] gives $H_0=G^+$. Consequently $Q=G^+G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda$ is an orthogonal projection and $\ker Q=\ker G$, so $\operatorname{Ran}(I-Q)=\ker G=\ker S$ by [F2]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The synthesis map of the canonical dual is $D=SG^+$ by [F1]. For any $X\in\mathsf H_d$, the spanning hypothesis [A1] supplies $c\in\mathbb R^m$ with $X=Sc$. Let $d,e\ge1$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A finite completely positive instrument from $\mathbb C^d$ to $\mathbb C^e$ is a family of completely positive complex-linear maps $I_a:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$, indexed by $a\in\mathcal A$, whose sum is trace-preserving. Then there are an integer $q\ge1$, an isometry $V:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e\otimes\mathbb C^q$, and pairwise orthogonal projections $Q_a$ on $\mathbb C^q$ with $\sum_aQ_a=I_q$ such that, for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$,
$$
I_a(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[(I_e\otimes Q_a)VXV^*(I_e\otimes Q_a)\right].
$$
Here $E=\mathbb C^q$ is the finite register space with its displayed orthonormal basis, and the partial trace is defined on its matrix units by $\operatorname{Tr}_E(Y\otimes|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{b,s}|)=\delta_{(a,r),(b,s)}Y$, extended linearly. The register basis is indexed by the Kraus labels $(a,r)$; a zero outcome map has no labels and corresponds to $Q_a=0$.

1.1 By [F1], each $I_a$ is completely positive in the finite matrix sense. Apply [F2] to obtain a finite Kraus family $(K_{a,r})_r$ for it, allowing the empty family for a zero map. Since $\mathcal A$ is finite, these finitely many choices require only finite choice. Put $q=\sum_aq_a$, where $q_a$ is the number of Kraus operators for outcome $a$. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The combined map $\sum_aI_a$ has Kraus family $(K_{a,r})_{a,r}$ and is trace-preserving by [A1] and [F1]. Thus [F2] gives $\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}^*K_{a,r}=I_d$. Since $d\ge1$, this identity implies $q\ge1$. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $(e_{a,r})_{a,r}$ be the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^q$ indexed by these labels. Define $Vx=\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}x\otimes e_{a,r}$ and $Q_a=\sum_r|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,r}|$. Then $V^*V=\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}^*K_{a,r}=I_d$, so $V$ is an isometry. Disjoint label sets make the $Q_a$ pairwise orthogonal and their sum $I_q$. [A1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Expanding the sandwich gives $\sum_{r,s}K_{a,r}XK_{a,s}^*\otimes|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,s}|$ with both labels restricted to outcome $a$. The partial trace sends each register matrix unit $|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,s}|$ to $\delta_{rs}$, leaving $\sum_rK_{a,r}XK_{a,r}^*=I_a(X)$ by step 1.1. This proves the claimed formula. [A1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite POVM on $\mathbb C^d$ whose real span is $\mathsf H_d$, and let $\rho\in\mathsf H_d$ satisfy $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_a)$, form the canonical dual $D_a$ from the Gram pseudoinverse, and write $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ for $D c=\sum_ac_aD_a$.

Define the frequency simplex $\Delta_m=\{f\in\mathbb R^m:f_a\ge0\text{ for all }a,\ \sum_af_a=1\}$ and the real-linear map $X:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ by $X(f)=\sum_af_aD_a$. On $\Delta_m$, this is the output of the previously defined linear-inversion procedure; on all of $\mathbb R^m$, $X$ denotes its linear extension. Use the induced operator norm $\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}=\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$.

Then exact probabilities reconstruct the state: $X(p)=\rho$. For every real frequency vector $f\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|f-p\|_2.
$$
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be measurable with the independent product law $\mathbb P(Y_1=a_1,\ldots,Y_n=a_n)=\prod_kp_{a_k}$ for every outcome tuple. Define $f_a=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le a\le m}|f_a-p_a|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
Consequently, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\sqrt m\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
These are conditional mathematical statements under the specified product sampling law; no empirical data or calibrated apparatus is asserted.
1.1 Apply [F1] with $H=\rho$. Then $\sum_ap_aD_a=\rho$, so [F3] gives $X(p)=\rho$. The probabilities are in $[0,1]$ and sum to one by [F2]. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For each sample $k$, $\sum_{a=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}=1$, so $f_a\ge0$ and $\sum_af_a=1$, as required by [F3]. Fix an outcome $a$ and set $Z_k^a=\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. For every $z\in\{0,1\}^n$, summing [A1] over the finite outcome tuples with $\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}=z_k$ gives $$\mathbb P(Z_1^a=z_1,\ldots,Z_n^a=z_n)=\prod_{k=1}^n\sum_{b:\,\mathbf1_{\{b=a\}}=z_k}p_b=\prod_{k=1}^n b_{p_a}(z_k),$$ since [F2] gives $\sum_bp_b=1$. Thus these indicators have the Bernoulli product law, and [F4] yields $\mathbb P(|f_a-p_a|\ge t)\le2e^{-2nt^2}$. No independence between indicators for different outcomes is used. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 By linearity, $X(f)-\rho=D(f-p)$. Set $C=(\sum_a\|D_a\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2)^{1/2}$. By [F7], this is the norm from a real inner product, so its triangle inequality follows from [F5] by expanding the square of a sum. Thus $\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\sum_a|c_a|\|D_a\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le C\|c\|_2$. Since $m\ge1$, the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^m$ contains $e_1$, so the set $\{\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:\|c\|_2=1\}$ is nonempty; the bound makes it bounded above. Its supremum exists by [F6] and is the finite induced operator norm in the Statement. Scaling $c$ (and treating $c=0$ directly) gives $\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|c\|_2$, which proves the deterministic estimate. [given, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A finite union bound gives $\mathbb P(\exists a:\ |f_a-p_a|\ge t)\le2m e^{-2nt^2}$. Set $t=\sqrt{\log(2m/\delta)/(2n)}$, which is positive since $2m/\delta>1$; then the right side is $\delta$. On the complementary event, $\|f-p\|_2\le\sqrt m\,t$, and step 2.1 gives the asserted state-error bound. [given, A1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i
e j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j
e i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E	o\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $
u=(
u_i)_{i\in E}$, meaning $
u_i\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in E}
u_i=1$; initial law $
u$ means $\mathbb P(Y_0=i)=
u_i$ for every $i\in E$. Put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and set $N_t=0$ for every $t\ge0$ and let the associated realization be the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim
u$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $
u$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. Under the Axiom of Choice, [[lem-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain-existence]] proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

owner_case_evidence.support_public_section:
## Example

On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$ and fix plus boundary spins $\sigma_x=+1$ whenever $\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n$. For $\sigma_x\in\{-1,+1\}$, define the finite-volume Ising Hamiltonian and Gibbs law by
$$H_{I,n}(\sigma)=-J_I\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\sigma_x\sigma_y,\qquad \mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma)\propto e^{-\beta H_{I,n}(\sigma)},\quad J_I>0.$$
Define $m_I^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma_0=+1)-1/2$ when the limit exists, and $\beta_c^I:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_I^+(\beta)>0\}$. The limit exists and
$$\beta_c^I J_I=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2).$$

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For each finite box and edge, [F1] gives $-J_P\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}=-(J_P/2)\sigma_x\sigma_y-J_P/2$. Setting $J_P=2J_I$ makes the finite Potts Hamiltonian equal to $H_{I,n}(\sigma)-J_I|E_n|$. The difference is independent of $\sigma$, so it cancels from the normalized finite Gibbs probabilities. The boundary color $1$ in the Potts model corresponds to the Ising plus spin $+1$. Thus the two models have the same plus-boundary probabilities and the same critical inverse temperature. [F1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Let $\beta_c^P$ and $\beta_c^I$ denote the critical inverse temperatures in the two definitions. Step 1.1 gives $\beta_c^I=\beta_c^P$. By [F2] with $J_P=2J_I$, $\beta_c^P(2J_I)=\log(1+\sqrt2)$. Divide by $2$ to obtain $\beta_c^I J_I=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$. This is an exact coupling conversion; the constant energy shift does not affect probabilities. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$ and fix plus boundary spins $\sigma_x=+1$ whenever $\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n$. For $\sigma_x\in\{-1,+1\}$, define the finite-volume Ising Hamiltonian and Gibbs law by
$$H_{I,n}(\sigma)=-J_I\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\sigma_x\sigma_y,\qquad \mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma)\propto e^{-\beta H_{I,n}(\sigma)},\quad J_I>0.$$
Define $m_I^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^{I,+}(\sigma_0=+1)-1/2$ when the limit exists, and $\beta_c^I:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_I^+(\beta)>0\}$. The limit exists and
$$\beta_c^I J_I=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2).$$

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For each finite box and edge, [F1] gives $-J_P\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}=-(J_P/2)\sigma_x\sigma_y-J_P/2$. The boundary color $1$ in the Potts model corresponds to the Ising plus spin $+1$. Thus the two models have the same plus-boundary probabilities and the same critical inverse temperature. [F1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Let $\beta_c^P$ and $\beta_c^I$ denote the critical inverse temperatures in the two definitions. Step 1.1 gives $\beta_c^I=\beta_c^P$. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $q\geq1$, put $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. The square-lattice free and wired cylinder-limit FK probability laws exist. For every $p>p_{\rm sd}(q)$, both have positive percolation probability. For every $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$, there are $C(p,q),c(p,q)>0$ such that every arbitrary-boundary cylinder-limit FK state $\phi$ satisfies
$$\phi(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z^2).$$
In particular, both percolation probabilities vanish below $p_{\rm sd}(q)$ and $p_c^0(q)=p_c^1(q)=p_{\rm sd}(q)$. These conclusions do not identify the free and wired measures at the critical parameter.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 By [A1] and [F1] the free and wired probability laws exist. In either law the events $D_r$ decrease with $r$. Their intersection is precisely the event that the origin cluster is unbounded: connection to every box boundary is equivalent to an unbounded cluster, and every finite path reaching a farther boundary contains an initial path to the nearer boundary. Countable additivity gives continuity from above, hence $\theta^b(p,q)=\inf_r\pi^b_p(D_r)=\Theta^b(p)$. This uses actual existing probability laws, rather than inferring their existence from consistent numerical cylinder weights. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Fix $p>p_{\rm sd}(q)$ and set $t=(p+p_{\rm sd}(q))/2$. Then $p_{\rm sd}(q)<t<p$. By [F2] and [F3], $\Theta^0(p)\geq\Theta^1(t)>0$, while [F3] directly gives $\Theta^1(p)>0$. Step 1.1 proves positive percolation for both laws at $p$. No equality of free and wired laws is used. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 For $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$ apply [F4]. In particular, each free or wired law satisfies the displayed bound. An origin path to $\partial\Lambda_r$ reaches one of its $8r$ vertices, each of Euclidean norm at least $r$. A finite union bound gives $\phi(D_r)\leq8rC(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)r}\to0$. Step 1.1 then gives zero percolation. Both defining infima are $p_{\rm sd}(q)$, since every parameter above it belongs to each positive-percolation set and none below it does. The bound for all other cylinder-limit states is already exactly [F4]. [F4, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

owner_case_evidence.support_public_section:
## Statement

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 Form the quotient vertex set $V_\xi$ by identifying each $\xi$-class. For an edge with distinct quotient endpoints $u,v$, let its incidence vector be $e_u+e_v\in\mathbb F_2^{V_\xi}$; a quotient loop has zero vector. In a component $C$ of the opened quotient graph $(V_\xi,A)$, every edge vector has even coordinate sum, so their span lies in the even-sum subspace, of dimension $|C|-1$. Conversely choose a root $r\in C$. For every $v\in C\setminus\{r\}$, connectedness [F2] gives an open path from $r$ to $v$; summing its edge vectors over $\mathbb F_2$ cancels each internal vertex twice and gives $e_r+e_v$. These $|C|-1$ vectors are linearly independent by their distinct $v$-coordinates. Thus the incidence rank on $C$ is $|C|-1$, and summing over components gives $r(A)=|V_\xi|-k_\xi(A)$, including isolated vertices and quotient loops. If $U_A$ and $U_C$ are the spans of incidence vectors from edge sets $A$ and $C$, then $U_{A\cup C}=U_A+U_C$ and $U_{A\cap C}\subseteq U_A\cap U_C$. The subspace dimension formula therefore gives $r(A)+r(C)\geq r(A\cup C)+r(A\cap C)$, hence $k_\xi(A\cup C)+k_\xi(A\cap C)\geq k_\xi(A)+k_\xi(C)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
support_paragraphs.1.2: 1.2 Fix the exterior edge states outside a finite $F\subseteq E$. For an interior edge set $A\subseteq F$, the total number of components of the combined graph is the number of exterior-only components disjoint from the boundary of $F$, plus the number of components of the graph on $F$ after identifying its boundary vertices that are connected by the fixed exterior open edges or by $\xi$. The first summand and all exterior edge factors are constant in $A$; they cancel when the conditional weights are normalized. Hence the conditional law on $F$ is exactly the finite FK law with this induced boundary partition. [F1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Since $|A\cup C|+|A\cap C|=|A|+|C|$, the factors $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}$ have equality in the lattice condition. The component inequality in step 1.1 and $q\geq1$ give the displayed log-supermodular inequality; every mass is positive by $0<p<1$ and $q\geq1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.2: 2.2 Given all edges except $e$, let $s$ be the conditional number of components when $e$ is closed. If its endpoints are already connected, opening it leaves $s$ unchanged, so open-to-closed odds are $p/(1-p)$ and the open probability is $p$. If the endpoints are not connected, opening it changes the component factor from $q^s$ to $q^{s-1}$, so the odds are $p/[q(1-p)]$ and the open probability is $p/(p+q(1-p))$. Both expressions increase with $p$; opening other edges or making the boundary partition coarser can only turn the second case into the first. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 We prove positive association for a strictly positive log-supermodular measure on $\{0,1\}^n$ by induction on $n$. It is trivial at $n=0$. For the last coordinate $s\in\{0,1\}$, each conditional measure $\mu_s$ on the first $n-1$ coordinates remains log-supermodular, so induction makes each $\mu_s$ positively associated. The ratio $R(x)=\mu(X_n=1,x)/\mu(X_n=0,x)$ is increasing in $x$: for $x\leq y$, apply log-supermodularity to $(y,0)$ and $(x,1)$ to obtain $R(y)\geq R(x)$. Thus for every increasing $h$, $\mathbb E_{\mu_1}h=\mathbb E_{\mu_0}(hR)/\mathbb E_{\mu_0}R\geq\mathbb E_{\mu_0}h$ by positive association under $\mu_0$. For increasing $f,g$, their conditional means $F_s=\mathbb E[f\mid X_n=s]$ and $G_s=\mathbb E[g\mid X_n=s]$ therefore satisfy $F_1\geq F_0$ and $G_1\geq G_0$. The conditional association and the nonnegative covariance of two increasing functions of the single Bernoulli coordinate give $\mathbb E(fg)\geq\sum_s\mu(X_n=s)F_sG_s\geq\mathbb E f\,\mathbb E g$. [step 2.1, algebra, induction]
support_paragraphs.4.1: 4.1 For two parameter/boundary choices ordered by $p_1\leq p_2$ and by refinement $\xi_1\leq\xi_2$, run random-scan heat-bath chains from the all-closed configuration, choosing the same edge and uniform random number at each update. Each update resamples one edge from its conditional FK law, so it preserves the corresponding FK law. Step 2.2 makes every coupled update preserve coordinatewise order. To prove marginal convergence, fix $j\in\{1,2\}$ and couple two copies of the chain with this same fixed kernel $(p_j,q,\xi_j)$, one from any configuration and one from its stationary FK law. If there are $r>0$ labels, a block of $r$ updates chooses them in a prescribed order with probability $r^{-r}$. If all its uniforms exceed $p_2<1$, every label is closed at the block end in both copies, regardless of their initial configurations. This event has probability $\delta=r^{-r}(1-p_2)^r>0$. Once these same-kernel copies meet they remain equal under shared updates. Independence of the update blocks bounds their disagreement probability after $k$ blocks by $(1-\delta)^k$, proving convergence of each marginal to its FK law. No absorbing equality is claimed between the different-kernel chains. For every increasing real $f$ on the finite configuration space, their order at every time gives $\mathbb E f(X_t^{(1)})\leq\mathbb E f(X_t^{(2)})$; taking the two marginal limits proves stochastic domination. When $r=0$ there is one configuration and the conclusion is immediate. [step 2.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the free finite-volume FK laws on $\Lambda_n$ are stochastically increasing under restriction as $n$ grows, and the wired finite-volume FK laws are stochastically decreasing under restriction. The probabilities of every finite-coordinate atom therefore have unique nonnegative normalized consistent numerical limits. Under Countable Choice, each limiting family extends uniquely to a probability measure on the cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra of $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$. Thus the free and wired infinite-volume states exist under this measure-extension hypothesis.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 Fix $n<m$ and condition the law on $E_m$ on every edge outside $E_n$. By [F1], the conditional law on $E_n$ is an FK law whose boundary partition records connections made by those fixed exterior edges. This partition is at least as wired as the free partition, so averaging the conditional laws gives $\phi^0_{m,p,q}|_{E_n}\geq_{st}\phi^0_{n,p,q}$. For the wired law on $E_m$, each induced partition on $\partial\Lambda_n$ is at most as wired as the one-class wired partition, so the same conditional comparison gives $\phi^1_{m,p,q}|_{E_n}\leq_{st}\phi^1_{n,p,q}$. [F1, F3, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 For each finite edge set $F\subset E_\infty$ and each $S\subseteq F$, the event that every edge in $S$ is open is increasing. Each limiting consistent family extends uniquely to a probability measure on the cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra; the same cylinder limits make it the unique subsequential limit of the corresponding sequence. Therefore the free and wired cylinder limits exist and are unique. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph, let $B\subseteq V$ have boundary partition $\xi$, fix $q\geq1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$, and let $\phi=\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ be the finite FK law. For every increasing event $A\subseteq2^E$ with $0<\phi(A)<1$ and $|E|\geq2$, define the conditional influence of edge $e$ by

$$I_A(e):=\phi(A\mid \omega_e=1)-\phi(A\mid\omega_e=0).$$

There is a constant $c(q,\varepsilon)>0$ such that

$$\max_{e\in E}I_A(e)\geq c(q,\varepsilon)\,\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\frac{\log|E|}{|E|}.$$

support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Label the edges $1,\ldots,n$. For a prefix $\eta$ put $a_r(\eta)=\phi(X_r=1\mid X_s=\eta_s,\ s<r)$ and $t_r(\eta)=1-a_r(\eta)$; positivity gives $0<t_r<1$. For $U\in[0,1]^n$ define recursively $\Phi_r(U)=\mathbf1_{\{U_r>t_r(\Phi_{<r}(U))\}}$. The first comparison in step 1.1 makes each $a_r$ increasing, so induction makes $\Phi$ coordinatewise increasing. For every $\omega\in\{0,1\}^n$, its exact inverse image is the box $Q_\omega=\prod_r I_r(\omega)$, where $I_r(\omega)=(t_r(\omega_{<r}),1]$ if $\omega_r=1$ and $I_r(\omega)=[0,t_r(\omega_{<r})]$ if $\omega_r=0$. Indeed membership in these intervals recursively forces exactly the prefix $\omega_{<r}$ and then bit $\omega_r$. These boxes form a disjoint partition of the entire cube, including all threshold values and endpoint faces. Their elementary volumes are $v_n(Q_\omega)=\prod_r a_r(\omega_{<r})^{\omega_r}(1-a_r(\omega_{<r}))^{1-\omega_r}=\phi(\omega)$ by the finite chain rule. Consequently $C=\Phi^{-1}(A)=\bigcup_{\omega\in A}Q_\omega$ is an increasing finite-box set of elementary volume $\phi(A)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1:
3.1 Fix $j$ and use the same uniforms attached to the same edge labels to construct $\Psi$ in order $j,1,\ldots,j-1,j+1,\ldots,n$. First set $U_j=1$. Both outputs have $j$th bit one. For $r<j$, suppose inductively $\Psi_{<r}\ge\Phi_{<r}$. The two comparisons in step 1.1 give
$$\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Psi_{<r},X_j=1)\ge\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r},X_j=1)\ge\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r}).$$
The common $U_r$ therefore gives $\Psi_r\ge\Phi_r$. After coordinate $j$, both constructions condition on the same set of previous labels, including $j=1$, with ordered values, so the first comparison alone continues the induction for $r>j$. Thus $\Psi(U_{-j},1)\ge\Phi(U_{-j},1)$ pointwise. With $U_j=0$, both $j$th bits are zero. For $r<j$, induction and the same two comparisons instead give
$$\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Psi_{<r},X_j=0)\le\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r},X_j=0)\le\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r}),$$
provided $\Psi_{<r}\le\Phi_{<r}$. For $r>j$ the first comparison continues this reversed order. Hence $\Psi(U_{-j},0)\le\Phi(U_{-j},0)$ pointwise as well. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]
support_paragraphs.4.1:
4.1 Since $A$ is increasing, the pointwise comparisons in step 3.1 imply, by elementary $(n-1)$-dimensional box integration,
$$F_j(C)\le\int\mathbf1_A(\Psi(U_{-j},1))\,dU_{-j}-\int\mathbf1_A(\Psi(U_{-j},0))\,dU_{-j}=I_A(j).$$
The equality follows from the finite conditional chain rule: after the first, forced bit $j$, the reordered algorithm samples the successive conditional probabilities given that bit. Its output inverse images and their sections are finite boxes, exactly as in step 2.1, so the displayed integrals are finite volume sums. These are literal endpoint evaluations of the defined maps, not conditioning a uniform variable on a null-probability event. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.5.1: 5.1 Apply [F3] to $C$ from step 2.1, with $n=|E|\ge2$ and $a=\phi(A)$. For some $j$ its endpoint influence is at least $\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\log n/(4n)$. Step 4.1 bounds that influence above by $I_A(j)$, proving the stated inequality with $c(q,\varepsilon)=1/4$. All conditional laws used exist for every real $q\ge1$ and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\subset(0,1)$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected plane graph with a fixed embedding and $|V|\geq1$. Use the free partition on all primal vertices, $B=V$. Its plane dual multigraph $G^*$ has one vertex for each face, including the unbounded face, and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; use the identity partition on the dual face-vertices. The unbounded face is one dual vertex, so this convention retains the exterior-face connection in the dual. For a primal open set $A\subseteq E$, let $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, so a dual edge is open exactly when its crossing primal edge is closed. For $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$ define $p^*\in(0,1)$ by

$$\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}=q\frac{1-p}{p}.$$

Then complementing the primal edges sends the finite FK law $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$ to the dual FK law $\phi_{G^*,p^*,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$: the random dual edge set $A^*$ has exactly that distribution. The unnormalized weight ratio is the configuration-independent factor $q^{|V|-1}((1-p)/p^*)^{|E|}$; the exponent $|V|-1$ includes the exterior-face contribution under this identity-partition convention.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For the spanning subgraph $(V,A)$, write $F_A$ for its faces. Starting with $A=E$, the dual open set is empty, so its components are the individual faces of $G$. Delete primal edges one at a time. If a deleted edge is a bridge of the current subgraph, its component count increases by one while its edge count decreases by one; [F3] therefore leaves the face count unchanged. By [F4] its two local sides lie in one current face, hence in one current dual component by induction, so adding its dual edge does not change the dual component count (the edge may be a loop in the original dual or may join vertices already connected by previously opened dual edges). If it is not a bridge, its component count is unchanged while its edge count decreases by one; [F3] therefore lowers the face count by one. By [F4], the edge has two distinct incident current faces, hence two distinct current dual components by induction; opening its dual edge merges exactly those components. Induction over the finitely many deleted edges proves that dual components correspond to faces of the current primal subgraph; in particular $k_{G^*}(A^*)=|F_A|$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra, induction]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Apply [F3] to $(V,A)$, whose number of components is $k_G(A)$. It gives $|V|-|A|+|F_A|=1+k_G(A)$. Substituting step 1.1 and rearranging yields $k_G(A)=k_{G^*}(A^*)+|V|-|A|-1$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 Let $a=|A|$ and $m=|E|$. ## Statement

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected plane graph with a fixed embedding and $|V|\geq1$. Use the free partition on all primal vertices, $B=V$. Its plane dual multigraph $G^*$ has one vertex for each face, including the unbounded face, and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; use the identity partition on the dual face-vertices. The unbounded face is one dual vertex, so this convention retains the exterior-face connection in the dual. For a primal open set $A\subseteq E$, let $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, so a dual edge is open exactly when its crossing primal edge is closed. For $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$ define $p^*\in(0,1)$ by

$$\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}=q\frac{1-p}{p}.$$

Then complementing the primal edges sends the finite FK law $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$ to the dual FK law $\phi_{G^*,p^*,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$: the random dual edge set $A^*$ has exactly that distribution. The defining relation for $p^*$ gives $p/[q(1-p^*)]=(1-p)/p^*$, so this ratio is $q^{|V|-1}((1-p)/p^*)^m$, independent of $A$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

## Statement

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $K\geq1$, and let $w_0,\ldots,w_K:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be finite positive weights. For each $k$, set $Z_k=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_k(x)$ and $\pi_k(x)=w_k(x)/Z_k$. For strictly positive probability mass functions $\nu,\mu:\mathsf T\to(0,1]$ on any finite nonempty set $\mathsf T$ (so $\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\nu(x)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\mu(x)=1$), define $\chi^2(\nu\Vert\mu)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\mu(x)(\nu(x)/\mu(x)-1)^2$. On a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $X_{k,j}:\Omega\to(\mathsf X,\mathcal P(\mathsf X))$ for $0\le k<K$ and $1\le j\le n_k$ be mutually independent random variables with $\mathbb P(X_{k,j}=x)=\pi_k(x)$ for each $x\in\mathsf X$, where $n_k\geq1$; these are the supplied stage samples in alg-csm-frontier-independent-bridge-ratios. Then

$$\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\frac{Z_K}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]}{(Z_K/Z_0)^2}=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\left(1+\frac{\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)}{n_k}\right).$$

Consequently, $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat R)/(Z_K/Z_0)^2$ is the displayed product minus $1$. This is an exact finite-sample result under independent exact draws; it gives no claim for reused trajectories, approximate Gibbs draws, or adaptively selected bridges.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For each $k$, apply [F1] to $(w_k,w_{k+1})$ and the $n_k$ independent samples with common law $\pi_k$. With $r_k=Z_{k+1}/Z_k$, the stage mean $\overline R_k$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=r_k$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)/r_k^2=\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. Since $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)+(\mathbb E[\overline R_k])^2$, it follows that $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2=1+\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. All moments are finite because $\mathsf X$ is finite and the weights are positive and finite. [F1, given, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Write $B_k=(X_{k,1},\ldots,X_{k,n_k})\in\mathsf X^{n_k}$. The blocks are independent finite-valued random elements, and $\overline R_k$ is a function of $B_k$. If $\mu_k(b)=\mathbb P(B_k=b)$, then for any functions $G_k$ of the respective blocks, independence and finite summation give $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}G_k(B_k)\right]=\sum_{b_0\in\mathsf X^{n_0},\ldots,b_{K-1}\in\mathsf X^{n_{K-1}}}\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mu_k(b_k)G_k(b_k)=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb E[G_k(B_k)].$$ Apply this first with $G_k=\overline R_k$ and then with $G_k=\overline R_k^2$. Thus $\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=\prod_k(Z_{k+1}/Z_k)=Z_K/Z_0$, while $\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]/(Z_K/Z_0)^2=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2$. Substitution from step 1.1 gives the stated product, and subtracting one yields the relative variance. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $K\geq1$, and let $w_0,\ldots,w_K:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be finite positive weights. For each $k$, set $Z_k=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_k(x)$ and $\pi_k(x)=w_k(x)/Z_k$. For strictly positive probability mass functions $\nu,\mu:\mathsf T\to(0,1]$ on any finite nonempty set $\mathsf T$ (so $\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\nu(x)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\mu(x)=1$), define $\chi^2(\nu\Vert\mu)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf T}\mu(x)(\nu(x)/\mu(x)-1)^2$. On a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $X_{k,j}:\Omega\to(\mathsf X,\mathcal P(\mathsf X))$ for $0\le k<K$ and $1\le j\le n_k$ be mutually independent random variables with $\mathbb P(X_{k,j}=x)=\pi_k(x)$ for each $x\in\mathsf X$, where $n_k\geq1$; these are the supplied stage samples in alg-csm-frontier-independent-bridge-ratios. Then

$$\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\frac{Z_K}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]}{(Z_K/Z_0)^2}=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\left(1+\frac{\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)}{n_k}\right).$$

Consequently, $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat R)/(Z_K/Z_0)^2$ is the displayed product minus $1$. This is an exact finite-sample result under independent exact draws; it gives no claim for reused trajectories, approximate Gibbs draws, or adaptively selected bridges.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 For each $k$, apply [F1] to $(w_k,w_{k+1})$ and the $n_k$ independent samples with common law $\pi_k$. With $r_k=Z_{k+1}/Z_k$, the stage mean $\overline R_k$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=r_k$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)/r_k^2=\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. Since $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)+(\mathbb E[\overline R_k])^2$, it follows that $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2=1+\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. All moments are finite because $\mathsf X$ is finite and the weights are positive and finite. [F1, given, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Write $B_k=(X_{k,1},\ldots,X_{k,n_k})\in\mathsf X^{n_k}$. The blocks are independent finite-valued random elements, and $\overline R_k$ is a function of $B_k$. If $\mu_k(b)=\mathbb P(B_k=b)$, then for any functions $G_k$ of the respective blocks, independence and finite summation give $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}G_k(B_k)\right]=\sum_{b_0\in\mathsf X^{n_0},\ldots,b_{K-1}\in\mathsf X^{n_{K-1}}}\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mu_k(b_k)G_k(b_k)=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb E[G_k(B_k)].$$ Apply this first with $G_k=\overline R_k$ and then with $G_k=\overline R_k^2$. Thus $\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=\prod_k(Z_{k+1}/Z_k)=Z_K/Z_0$, while $\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]/(Z_K/Z_0)^2=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2$. Substitution from step 1.1 gives the stated product, and subtracting one yields the relative variance. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

This is the homogeneous-equilibrium, fixed-mean torus variational result for the defined continuum action.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every real $q\geq1$, put $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. For every $p>p_{\rm sd}(q)$, the wired state has $\theta^1(p,q)>0$; for every $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$, both free and wired states have zero percolation probability and the free and wired critical thresholds defined in [[def-csm-frontier-fk-infinite-volume-states]] equal $p_{\rm sd}(q)$. For every $p<p_{\rm sd}(q)$, there are constants $C(p,q),c(p,q)>0$ such that every cylinder-limit FK state $\phi$ on $\mathbb Z^2$ satisfies
$$\phi(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb Z^2).$$
No equality of the free and wired measures at $p=p_{\rm sd}(q)$, critical exponent, or order of transition is asserted.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 Fix $q\geq1$ and write $p_s=p_{\rm sd}(q)$. By [F2], $\theta^1(p,q)>0$ for every $p>p_s$ and $\theta^1(p,q)=0$ for every $p<p_s$. Therefore the infimum defining $p_c^1(q)$ is $p_s$: no parameter below $p_s$ belongs to the defining set, while every parameter above $p_s$ does. [F1, F2, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 The free/wired threshold-coincidence conclusion in [F2] gives $p_c^0(q)=p_c^1(q)=p_s$. This is a statement about the two infima; it does not identify the measures or their percolation probabilities at $p=p_s$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 For $p<p_s$, [F2] supplies constants $C(p,q),c(p,q)>0$ for the wired two-point function. The same crossing-amplification result proves that every cylinder-limit state is stochastically dominated by the wired state on connection events, so the identical bound holds for every $\phi$ in the statement. The stated choice hypothesis is the one used by the supplier to construct the probability laws and its countable subcritical coupling. [F2] ∎

## Statement

For each $q\geq1$ and aspect ratio $\alpha>1$, there is a constant $c(\alpha,q)>0$ such that the following holds. Let $n,m$ be positive integers with $m>\lceil\alpha n\rceil$, let $T_m=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$ with its nearest-neighbor horizontal and vertical edges and periodic boundary conditions, and give its edges the FK law with no boundary wiring, parameter $q$, and $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. The probability of a horizontal open crossing of the vertex rectangle $\{0,\ldots,\lceil\alpha n\rceil\}\times\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is at least $c(\alpha,q)$, uniformly in $n$ and $m$.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 The invertible linear map $u=x+y$, $v=y-x$ sends the ordinary square lattice to $P$ and its nearest-neighbor edges to the diagonal edges. Its inverse is $x=(u-v)/2$, $y=(u+v)/2$. Ordinary periods $(m,0),(0,m)$ become $(m,-m),(m,m)$, generating exactly the diagonal-period lattice in [F4]. It is therefore a labelled graph isomorphism, preserving the weights in [F1]. A rotated patch with both coordinate spans less than $m$ embeds: every nonzero period has at least one coordinate of absolute value at least $m$. We may compute probabilities of such patches in these coordinates. The cellular torus comparison [F3] is the likelihood input used in [F4], not an unproved planar substitution for torus topology. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]
support_paragraphs.1.2: 1.2 A closed rotated vertical rectangle of width $S\in4\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and height $2S$ has crossing probability at least $d=b^2a$ if $2S<m$. Indeed take the vertical crossings of $[0,S]\times[0,3S/2]$ and $[0,S]\times[S/2,2S]$, and a horizontal crossing of their overlap square $[0,S]\times[S/2,3S/2]$. The vertical bounds are [F4] after coordinate interchange; the shift $S/2$ is even and preserves $P$. The square bound is also [F4]. Each horizontal path intersects both vertical paths by [F5], so their union gives the required vertical crossing. FKG [F2] gives $b^2a$. Translation by any integer vector with even coordinate sum preserves the lattice, the periodic FK law, and this estimate. Restricting a taller crossing at its first hit of any intermediate integer height gives a crossing of the truncated rectangle. [F2, F4, F5, construct, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1:
2.1 Suppose $n\geq32$. Set $k=\lfloor n/32\rfloor$, $L=16k$, $h=4k=L/4$, $W=\lceil\alpha n\rceil$ and $J=\lceil W/h\rceil$. For $0\leq j\leq J$ put $a_j=jh$, $b_j=-jh$, and take the closed squares
$$Q_j=[a_j,a_j+L]\times[b_j,b_j+L].$$
For $0\leq j<J$ take the closed connectors
$$C_j=[a_j+h,a_j+L]\times[b_j-h,b_j+L].$$
Each connector has width $12k$ and height $20k$. Since $a_j+b_j=0$, every vertex of every square and connector has original coordinate $0\leq y=(u+v)/2\leq L\leq n$. The corner translations $(jh,-jh)$ preserve $P$. Every square embeds and has horizontal crossing probability at least $a$ by [F4], since $L<m$. A vertical aspect-two rectangle of the same connector width $S=12k$, starting at its bottom, has height $24k<n<m$. Step 1.2 bounds its vertical crossing probability below by $d$. ## Statement

Let $\mathsf X$ be finite and nonempty, let $w:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be an exact finite positive weight, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be a finite observable. Suppose the finite rational input intervals in the definition of alg-csm-frontier-interval-finite-partition contain every exact $w(x)$ and $f(x)$. The algorithm terminates after finitely many operations. If it returns finite intervals $\mathcal Z$ and $\mathcal N$, then they contain $Z=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w(x)$ and $N=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w(x)f(x)$, respectively. If it also returns an expectation interval $\mathcal E$, then its denominator interval has positive lower endpoint and $\mathcal E$ contains the exact normalized expectation $\sum_x\pi(x)f(x)=N/Z$, where $\pi(x)=w(x)/Z$. An overflow, non-finite operation, or nonpositive denominator lower endpoint produces an unresolved status and carries no normalized-expectation enclosure claim.

support_paragraphs.1.1: 1.1 The finite enumeration supplies one input interval for each exact weight and observable. By [F2] and [F5], when endpoint conversion is finite, rounding the lower endpoint down and upper endpoint up preserves containment of each input interval; if conversion overflows, the algorithm returns unresolved and the theorem makes no finite-enclosure claim. The partition sum and weighted sum are finite acyclic expression DAGs by [F1] and [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, construct]
support_paragraphs.2.1: 2.1 Order the nodes of each finite DAG topologically. Each input node encloses its exact value by step 1.1. At every operation node with a finite result, [F4] gives the interval extension prescribed for that operation and [F6] proves that its value encloses the exact operation on the predecessor values. Induction over the finite node order therefore places $Z$ in $\mathcal Z$ and $N$ in $\mathcal N$ whenever those intervals are returned. [F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, given]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 The exact partition sum satisfies $Z>0$ because $\mathsf X$ is nonempty and every $w(x)>0$. If the returned lower endpoint of $\mathcal Z$ is positive, then $0\notin\mathcal Z$ and [F4] defines outward interval division; applying [F6] to this final operation gives $N/Z\in\mathcal N/\mathcal Z=\mathcal E$. If the lower endpoint is nonpositive, or any operation is non-finite, [F1] returns an unresolved status and no quotient enclosure is claimed. Finally, the procedure performs finitely many conversions and finitely many operations because $\mathsf X$ is finite, and every operation returns a finite interval or a status; hence it terminates. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, given, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set equipped with counting measure. For $a\in\{0,1\}$, let $w_a:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be a finite positive weight, define $Z_a=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_a(x)$, and define the probability mass function $\pi_a(x)=w_a(x)/Z_a$. For an integer $n\geq1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables with common law $\pi_0$. Define $R(x)=w_1(x)/w_0(x)$, $\widehat r_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nR(X_j)$, and $\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x)-1)^2$. Then

$$\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[\widehat r_n]=\frac{Z_1}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_0}(\widehat r_n)}{(Z_1/Z_0)^2}=\frac{\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)}{n}.$$

The estimator uses only the finite raw-weight ratios $w_1(X_j)/w_0(X_j)$; the partition sums define the target ratio and probability laws but are not inputs to its computation.

Since $w_0(x),w_1(x)>0$ on every point of $\mathsf X$, the formal ordinary-importance-sampling setup with counting measure, $\tilde p=w_1$, $q=\pi_0$, $f\equiv1$, and $Z_p=Z_1$ has full support and finite weighted second moment. $$\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[\widehat r_n]=\frac{Z_1}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_0}(\widehat r_n)}{(Z_1/Z_0)^2}=\frac{\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)}{n}.$$

## Statement

Let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, $J>0$, and $\beta>0$. On $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\lVert x\rVert_\infty=n\}$ and let $E_n$ be the nearest-neighbor edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$. The $Q$-state Potts model has spins $\sigma:\Lambda_n\to\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, fixed plus boundary $\sigma|_{B_n}=1$, and finite-volume Gibbs probabilities proportional to $e^{-\beta H_n(\sigma)}$, where
$$H_n(\sigma)=-J\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}.$$
Define its plus-boundary order parameter by
$$m_Q^+(\beta):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^+(\sigma_0=1)-Q^{-1},$$
when the limit exists, and define $\beta_c:=\inf\{\beta>0:m_Q^+(\beta)>0\}$. Then the limit exists and
$$\beta_c J=\log(1+\sqrt Q).$$
This is a numerical limit of finite-volume probabilities; no infinite-volume probability-law extension is required.

support_paragraphs.1.1:
1.1 Put $v=e^{\beta J}-1$ and $p=v/(1+v)=1-e^{-\beta J}$. On the finite spin-edge configurations with $\sigma|_{B_n}=1$, define the joint weight
$$W_n^+(\sigma,A)=v^{|A|}\prod_{\{x,y\}\in A}\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}}.$$
For fixed $\sigma$, summing over $A\subseteq E_n$ gives $\prod_{e\in E_n}(1+v\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_x=\sigma_y\}})=e^{-\beta H_n(\sigma)}$. For fixed $A$, every component meeting $B_n$ has color $1$ and each remaining component has $Q$ choices. After wiring all of $B_n$ into one class, the number of unpinned components is $k_{\xi_n}(A)-1$. Thus the edge marginal has weight $Q^{k_{\xi_n}(A)-1}v^{|A|}$, proportional by the configuration-independent factor $Q^{-1}$ to the wired FK weight in [F3]. Normalization therefore gives exactly the finite wired FK law. This supplies the pinned version of [F2] by an explicit finite sum. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]
support_paragraphs.2.1:
2.1 Conditional on $A$, the origin has color $1$ with probability one if it connects to $B_n$, and with probability $1/Q$ otherwise. Indeed every unpinned component has its independent uniform color by the finite count of step 1.1. Consequently
$$\mathbb P_{\beta,n}^+(\sigma_0=1)=Q^{-1}+(1-Q^{-1})a_n(p,Q).$$
By [F4] the right side has a numerical limit. Hence $m_Q^+(\beta)=(1-Q^{-1})L(1-e^{-\beta J},Q)$. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]
support_paragraphs.3.1: 3.1 The map $\beta\mapsto1-e^{-\beta J}$ is strictly increasing from $0$ to $1$. By [F4] and the positive prefactor in step 2.1, $m_Q^+(\beta)$ is zero below the unique parameter solving $1-e^{-\beta J}=\sqrt Q/(1+\sqrt Q)$ and positive above it. Its defining positive-set infimum is therefore that parameter, regardless of its value at the critical point. Solving gives $e^{-\beta_cJ}=1/(1+\sqrt Q)$ and $\beta_cJ=\log(1+\sqrt Q)$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

support.exact_paragraph: The Gaussian integral [F5] and the positive scaling in [F8] give $\|\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\|_2^2=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\int e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon}dx=1$. In its Wigner integral, the product of the two Gaussian factors is $ (\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{\epsilon}-\frac{y^2}{4\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ipy}{\epsilon}\right). $ Multiplying by $e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}$ and applying [F3] with $\eta=\xi-p$ gives $ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon} 2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-(\xi-p)^2/\epsilon}, $ which is the stated nonnegative density. Its integral is $1$ by [F5] and [F8]. For its phase-space moments, apply [F8] to $x=q+\sqrt\epsilon s$ and $\xi=p+\sqrt\epsilon r$. The centered first moments vanish because $s e^{-s^2}$ and $r e^{-r^2}$ are odd; the cross-moment vanishes for the same reason. Integration by parts [F5] gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\frac12\int e^{-s^2}ds$, so each centered variance is $\epsilon/2$. This verifies the mean and covariance definitions in the Statement. For the operator uncertainties, direct differentiation gives $P\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=\bigl(p+i(x-q)\bigr)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$, while $Q\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=x\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$. Thus $\bar Q_\psi=q$, $\bar P_\psi=p$, and the two squared standard deviations are both $\int(x-q)^2|\psi|^2dx=\epsilon/2$ by the same Gaussian integration by parts. To prove the lower bound for every normalized $\varphi\in\mathcal S$, first note that $Q$ and $P$ are symmetric on $\mathcal S$: for $P$ this is [F5] applied to decaying Schwartz factors, and for $Q$ it follows from real multiplication. Hence $\bar Q_\varphi,\bar P_\varphi\in\mathbb R$. Put $A=Q-\bar Q_\varphi I$ and $B=P-\bar P_\varphi I$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F6], the commutator $[A,B]=[Q,P]=i\epsilon I$ from [F2], and symmetry give $ \Delta_\varphi Q\,\Delta_\varphi P\ge|\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|=\frac12|\langle[A,B]\varphi,\varphi\rangle|=\frac\epsilon2. $ Indeed, under the first-variable-linear convention, $\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle=\langle BA\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ and its conjugate is $\langle AB\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. Thus the Gaussian attains the lower bound. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

The classical Hamilton equations for $h(x,\xi)=(x^2+\xi^2)/2$ solve to $ \Phi_t(x,\xi)=(x\cos t+\xi\sin t,\ \xi\cos t-x\sin t). $ This matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $\Phi_t(q,p)=(q_t,p_t)$. For $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, [F4] gives $ \langle W_t,a\rangle =\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^2}a(\Phi_t z)W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](z)\,dz, $ where the last equality is [F2]. The integrand is in $L^1$ because $a$ is compactly supported and the Gaussian is integrable. Apply [F8] to the rotation $z'=\Phi_tz$; its determinant is $1$, so the resulting density is $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](\Phi_{-t}z')$. Orthogonality gives $ |\Phi_{-t}(x,\xi)-(q,p)|^2 =|(x,\xi)-\Phi_t(q,p)|^2, $ so this density is exactly the displayed $W_t$. The same change of variables sends its mean $(q,p)$ to $(q_t,p_t)$ and transforms covariance as $R_t(\epsilon I_2/2)R_t^T=\epsilon I_2/2$, since $R_t$ is orthogonal. This proves the asserted exact transport and covariance for every compactly supported smooth test symbol and hence for the distributional Wigner functional defined in the Statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F4, F8, algebra] ∎

$$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}\,dy $$

for $u,v\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, and define the Weyl operator initially as the form

$$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi . $$

There is a unique bounded operator $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ representing this form, and

$$ \|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq C_d\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty , $$

where $C_d$ depends only on $d$. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, this extension agrees with the kernel definition in [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner].. Root adopts and binds this actual semantic disposition to the current item and row; this is not independent proof acceptance.

support.exact_paragraph: Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. The same holds with $Z,Z'$ interchanged. Thus the integral kernel $$ K_\epsilon(Z,Z'):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon) $$ has uniformly bounded row and column $L^1$ norms, each at most $C_dD(a)$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$, Tonelli [F4] and the column bound show that $\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2dZ'$ is finite for almost every $Z$. For each such $Z$, write $$ \int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'=\int\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\,\frac{K_\epsilon(Z,Z')}{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}f(Z')\,dZ', $$ using quotient $0$ where $K_\epsilon=0$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] in $L^2(dZ')$ yields $$ |\int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'|^2\leq(\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|\,dZ')\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2\,dZ'. $$ Integrating in $Z$ and using Tonelli [F4] and the column bound yields $\|K_\epsilon f\|_2\leq C_dD(a)\|f\|_2$. Applying this estimate to step 2.1 and using the isometry in step 1.1 proves $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\leq C_dD(a)\|V_\epsilon u\|_2\|V_\epsilon v\|_2=C_dD(a)\|u\|_2\|v\|_2 . $$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, F4, F12, algebra]

For fixed $u\in\mathcal S$, the bounded form in step 3.1 extends continuously in $v$ to $L^2$, which is a Hilbert space by [F6], and $v\mapsto\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}$ is a bounded linear functional there. Riesz representation [F7] gives a unique $y\in L^2$ with $\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}=\langle v,y\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$; conjugate symmetry gives $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=\langle y,v\rangle$, so set $A_\epsilon u=y$. Its norm is at most $C_dD(a)\|u\|_2$. Uniqueness makes $u\mapsto A_\epsilon u$ linear on $\mathcal S$, and [F11] makes its extension to all of $L^2$ unique. Hence the operator norm is at most $C_dD(a)$. [given, A1, step 3.1, F6, F7, F11, algebra] ∎

support.exact_paragraph: Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. The same holds with $Z,Z'$ interchanged. Thus the integral kernel $$ K_\epsilon(Z,Z'):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon) $$ has uniformly bounded row and column $L^1$ norms, each at most $C_dD(a)$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$, Tonelli [F4] and the column bound show that $\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2dZ'$ is finite for almost every $Z$. For each such $Z$, write $$ \int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'=\int\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\,\frac{K_\epsilon(Z,Z')}{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}f(Z')\,dZ', $$ using quotient $0$ where $K_\epsilon=0$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] in $L^2(dZ')$ yields $$ |\int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'|^2\leq(\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|\,dZ')\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2\,dZ'. $$ Integrating in $Z$ and using Tonelli [F4] and the column bound yields $\|K_\epsilon f\|_2\leq C_dD(a)\|f\|_2$. Applying this estimate to step 2.1 and using the isometry in step 1.1 proves $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\leq C_dD(a)\|V_\epsilon u\|_2\|V_\epsilon v\|_2=C_dD(a)\|u\|_2\|v\|_2 . $$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, F4, F12, algebra]

For fixed $u\in\mathcal S$, the bounded form in step 3.1 extends continuously in $v$ to $L^2$, which is a Hilbert space by [F6], and $v\mapsto\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}$ is a bounded linear functional there. Riesz representation [F7] gives a unique $y\in L^2$ with $\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}=\langle v,y\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$; conjugate symmetry gives $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=\langle y,v\rangle$, so set $A_\epsilon u=y$. Its norm is at most $C_dD(a)\|u\|_2$. Uniqueness makes $u\mapsto A_\epsilon u$ linear on $\mathcal S$, and [F11] makes its extension to all of $L^2$ unique. Hence the operator norm is at most $C_dD(a)$. [given, A1, step 3.1, F6, F7, F11, algebra] ∎

If $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$, its $L^1$ norm is $1$, hence $|B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq\|a\|_\infty$. If $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$, then $$ L_\delta:= rac{\epsilon}{i|\delta|^2}
abla_w\phi_\delta\cdot
abla_w,\qquad \phi_\delta(w):=-\sigma(w,\delta) $$ satisfies $L_\delta e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}=e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}$, since $|
abla_w\phi_\delta|=|\delta|$. Integrating by parts $N_d$ times against the Gaussian is justified coordinatewise by [F10] and Fubini [F5]: derivatives of the Gaussian are integrable, derivatives of $a$ are bounded, and the Gaussian forces the endpoint products to vanish. Translation $w=z-m$ and scaling $w=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ in these absolutely integrable terms are justified by [F9]. Each derivative on the Gaussian contributes a factor bounded by $\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$; a derivative on $a$ contributes $\epsilon/|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$, since $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\leq1$. Put $c=2\pi\epsilon>0$ and define $D_cg(\xi)=c^{-d/2}g(\xi/c)$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$. A null set is sent to a null set by the same change-of-variables theorem [F2], so this definition is independent of the representative of $g$. Apply [F2] to $T(\eta)=c\eta$, whose Jacobian determinant is $c^d$, and to the nonnegative function $f(\xi)=|g(\xi/c)|^2$. This gives
$$ \|D_cg\|_2^2=c^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\xi/c)|^2\,d\xi =c^{-d}c^d\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(\eta)|^2\,d\eta =\|g\|_2^2. $$
The inverse is $D_{1/c}$, as direct substitution shows, so $D_c$ is unitary. [given, A1, F2, algebra]

By [F3], $\mathcal F_\epsilon u=D_c\mathcal F_2u$ for every $u\in\mathcal S$. Both factors extend unitarily by step 1.1 and [F1], so their composition is a unitary extension to $L^2$. If $G$ were another continuous extension, then $D_c^{-1}G$ would be a continuous extension of $\mathcal F_2$; uniqueness in [F1] gives $D_c^{-1}G=\mathcal F_2$, hence $G=D_c\mathcal F_2$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

support.exact_paragraph: For $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz in $(x,y)$. Differentiating under its integral and multiplying by powers of $x$ leaves absolutely integrable products of Schwartz functions, so $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself. Apply [F5] on $\mathcal S$ to obtain the bounded identity $ \frac{i}{\epsilon}[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)] =\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{b,h\})+\epsilon^2\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,b,V}). $ The right side is bounded by [F5] and [F6]. For each $u\in D(H_\epsilon)$, [A2] supplies $u_n\in\mathcal S$ with $\|u_n-u\|_2^2+\|H_\epsilon u_n-H_\epsilon u\|_2^2\to0$. Boundedness of $\operatorname{Op}(b)$ and of the commutator makes both $\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n$ and $H_\epsilon\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n=\operatorname{Op}(b)H_\epsilon u_n+[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(b)]u_n$ converge; closedness of the self-adjoint $H_\epsilon$ gives $\operatorname{Op}(b)u\in D(H_\epsilon)$ and the identity there. For $\psi\in D(H_\epsilon)$, differentiate $ F(s)\psi:=U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a_s)U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $ The domain preservation in [F4] and step 1.2 justify the product rule in $L^2$; the symbol derivative in step 2.1 is also an operator-norm derivative by [F6], since the symbols and their difference quotients have common compact support and converge with all derivatives required by that estimate. The two Hamiltonian terms combine to $U_\epsilon(s)^*(i/\epsilon)[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(a_s)]U_\epsilon(s)$; $\partial_s\operatorname{Op}(a_s)=-\operatorname{Op}(\{a_s,h\})$ cancels its Poisson term by step 1.2. The remainder estimate [F5] followed by [F6] consequently yields $ \sup_{|s|,|t|\le T}\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})\|\le C_{T,V,a}. $ The derivative must also be continuous up to the endpoints to use [F7]. The local remainder formula in [[lem-nrqmx-cubic-moyal-commutator-remainder]] is linear in its symbol argument. For fixed $t$, the symbols $a_s$ have common compact support on the interval and vary continuously in every Schwartz seminorm by step 2.1; applying the remainder estimate to $a_s-a_{s'}$ and then [F6] shows $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})-\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_{s'},V})\|\to0$ as $s'\to s$. Thus the remainder operators are norm-continuous. Strong continuity of $U_\epsilon(s)$ and its adjoint, together with uniform boundedness of these operators, makes $s\mapsto U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})U_\epsilon(s)\psi$ continuous for each fixed $\psi$. The derivative in the displayed formula therefore extends continuously to both endpoints. Integrate it by [F7], use unitarity, and evaluate the endpoints $F(t)\psi=U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi$ and $F(0)\psi=\operatorname{Op}(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi$. Differentiating under its integral and multiplying by powers of $x$ leaves absolutely integrable products of Schwartz functions, so $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself. Apply [F5] on $\mathcal S$ to obtain the bounded identity $ \frac{i}{\epsilon}[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)] =\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{b,h\})+\epsilon^2\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,b,V}). $ The right side is bounded by [F5] and [F6]. For each $u\in D(H_\epsilon)$, [A2] supplies $u_n\in\mathcal S$ with $\|u_n-u\|_2^2+\|H_\epsilon u_n-H_\epsilon u\|_2^2\to0$. Boundedness of $\operatorname{Op}(b)$ and of the commutator makes both $\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n$ and $H_\epsilon\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n=\operatorname{Op}(b)H_\epsilon u_n+[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(b)]u_n$ converge; closedness of the self-adjoint $H_\epsilon$ gives $\operatorname{Op}(b)u\in D(H_\epsilon)$ and the identity there. For $\psi\in D(H_\epsilon)$, differentiate $ F(s)\psi:=U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a_s)U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $ The domain preservation in [F4] and step 1.2 justify the product rule in $L^2$; the symbol derivative in step 2.1 is also an operator-norm derivative by [F6], since the symbols and their difference quotients have common compact support and converge with all derivatives required by that estimate. The two Hamiltonian terms combine to $U_\epsilon(s)^*(i/\epsilon)[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(a_s)]U_\epsilon(s)$; $\partial_s\operatorname{Op}(a_s)=-\operatorname{Op}(\{a_s,h\})$ cancels its Poisson term by step 1.2. Step2.1 proves that a finite-order denominator zero plus nonvanishing numerator implies a pole of exactly that order. These explicit local hypotheses are sufficient; the theorem claims neither existence of a denominator zero for every coupling nor a universal converse from every resonance to these test-vector data. Pairing the rank-one identity [A1] against $f,h$ and using the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\langle R_\lambda(z)f,h\rangle
=\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle-\frac{\lambda\,a_f(z)b_h(z)}{d(z)}$.
Each numerator term has the holomorphic continuation assumed in the Statement, so the right side defines the corresponding meromorphic continuation on $D$. [A1, given, F1, algebra]

By the finite-order zero hypothesis, $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=(z-z_0)^k q(z)$ near $z_0$, where $q$ is holomorphic and $q(z_0)\ne0$. The product $a_f b_h$ is holomorphic and nonzero at $z_0$, so its quotient by $d_{\mathrm{cont}}$ has a pole of order exactly $k$. The first term $\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle_{\mathrm{cont}}$ is holomorphic and cannot cancel that pole. Thus the continued $H_\lambda$ matrix element has the asserted resonance pole. If $k=1$, its residue is $-\lambda a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/d'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/m'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)$. [step 1.2, given, F1, algebra]

In the Gaussian model take exactly the positive center $E_\star$, disk excluding zero, and normalized holomorphic branch $k_D$ specified in [F2]. Its formula therefore supplies the assumed holomorphic continuation on this $D$, not a continuation across the threshold zero or a differently signed sheet. Choose a Borel representative of $|u|^2$ by [F6]. The PVM formula [F4] and polar integration [F5] then give, for every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$,
$\mu_u(B)=\int_{\{|p|^2\in B\}}|u(p)|^2\,dp
=\int_{B\cap(0,\infty)}\frac{\sqrt E}{2}
\int_{S^2}|u(\sqrt E\,\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dE$.
The substitution $E=r^2$ gives $r^2\,dr=(\sqrt E/2)\,dE$. Thus $E_{H_0}(N)=0$ for every Lebesgue-null $N\subset(0,\infty)$, so any open $I\subset(0,\infty)$ meets the Statement's absolute-continuity condition. For $f=h=g$, one has $a_g=b_g=m_{\mathrm{cont}}$. At a zero of $1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}$, $m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-1/\lambda\ne0$. Hence the noncancellation condition of step 2.1 holds at every finite-order zero, proving the stated Gaussian specialization. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

If a nonzero vector $u\in D(H_\lambda)$ satisfied $H_\lambda u=z_0u$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_0<0$, self-adjointness in [A1] would make $\langle H_\lambda u,u\rangle$ real, but it equals $z_0\|u\|^2$, which is nonreal. This contradiction proves that the continued pole is not a nonreal eigenvalue. [A1, algebra] ∎

Pairing the rank-one identity [A1] against $f,h$ and using the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\langle R_\lambda(z)f,h\rangle
=\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle-\frac{\lambda\,a_f(z)b_h(z)}{d(z)}$.
Each numerator term has the holomorphic continuation assumed in the Statement, so the right side defines the corresponding meromorphic continuation on $D$. [A1, given, F1, algebra]

By the finite-order zero hypothesis, $d_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=(z-z_0)^k q(z)$ near $z_0$, where $q$ is holomorphic and $q(z_0)\ne0$. The product $a_f b_h$ is holomorphic and nonzero at $z_0$, so its quotient by $d_{\mathrm{cont}}$ has a pole of order exactly $k$. The first term $\langle R_0(z)f,h\rangle_{\mathrm{cont}}$ is holomorphic and cannot cancel that pole. Thus the continued $H_\lambda$ matrix element has the asserted resonance pole. If $k=1$, its residue is $-\lambda a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/d'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-a_f(z_0)b_h(z_0)/m'_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)$. [step 1.2, given, F1, algebra]

In the Gaussian model take exactly the positive center $E_\star$, disk excluding zero, and normalized holomorphic branch $k_D$ specified in [F2]. Its formula therefore supplies the assumed holomorphic continuation on this $D$, not a continuation across the threshold zero or a differently signed sheet. Choose a Borel representative of $|u|^2$ by [F6]. The PVM formula [F4] and polar integration [F5] then give, for every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$,
$\mu_u(B)=\int_{\{|p|^2\in B\}}|u(p)|^2\,dp
=\int_{B\cap(0,\infty)}\frac{\sqrt E}{2}
\int_{S^2}|u(\sqrt E\,\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dE$.
The substitution $E=r^2$ gives $r^2\,dr=(\sqrt E/2)\,dE$. Thus $E_{H_0}(N)=0$ for every Lebesgue-null $N\subset(0,\infty)$, so any open $I\subset(0,\infty)$ meets the Statement's absolute-continuity condition. For $f=h=g$, one has $a_g=b_g=m_{\mathrm{cont}}$. At a zero of $1+\lambda m_{\mathrm{cont}}$, $m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z_0)=-1/\lambda\ne0$. Hence the noncancellation condition of step 2.1 holds at every finite-order zero, proving the stated Gaussian specialization. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

If a nonzero vector $u\in D(H_\lambda)$ satisfied $H_\lambda u=z_0u$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_0<0$, self-adjointness in [A1] would make $\langle H_\lambda u,u\rangle$ real, but it equals $z_0\|u\|^2$, which is nonreal. This contradiction proves that the continued pole is not a nonreal eigenvalue. [A1, algebra] ∎

Derivatives of $e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}$ contribute powers of $\lambda+\mu$. Since $T_\lambda^\epsilon$ is unitary, $\langle T_\mu^\epsilon u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle=\langle T_\lambda^\epsilon T_\mu^\epsilon u,v\rangle$; the double integral is absolutely convergent with majorant $(2\pi)^{-4d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|\widehat b\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, so Fubini and the Weyl relation give $$ c_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,d\lambda\,d\mu . $$ The phase-space Fourier coefficient of $\{a,b\}$ is $-\sigma(\lambda,\mu)\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)$; this follows by differentiating the Fourier modes in the explicitly fixed Poisson convention. Fix $\lambda,\mu$ and write $f(s)=e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}$, a $C^2$ complex function on $[0,1]$. Applying [F10] to the real and imaginary parts twice gives $f(1)-f(0)=\int_0^1f'(r)\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1\int_0^r f''(s)\,ds\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1(1-s)f''(s)\,ds$; the last equality is Fubini [F5] on the continuous integrand over the triangle. Since $f'(0)=-i\epsilon\sigma/2$ and $f''(s)=-\epsilon^2\sigma^2e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}/4$, this derives $$ e^{-i\epsilon\sigma/2}=1-\frac{i\epsilon\sigma}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^2\sigma^2}{4}\int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}\,ds. $$ Set $$ R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu):=\frac{\sigma(\lambda,\mu)^2}{4} \int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,ds . $$ Consequently the symbol remainder is $$ r_\epsilon(z)=-(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)\,d\lambda\,d\mu. $$ For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ with $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le K:=4d+4$, differentiate $|\alpha|$ times in $z$ and integrate by parts $|\beta|$ times in $\lambda$ using [F9] coordinatewise to estimate $z^\beta\partial_z^\alpha r_\epsilon(z)$. Each integration is justified because the Fourier factors and all their derivatives have rapid decay and every differentiated factor has at most polynomial growth; thus the derivative products are integrable and boundary products vanish. Each $\lambda$-derivative of the remainder factor is bounded by $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)|\le C_\gamma\langle\lambda\rangle^2\langle\mu\rangle^{|\gamma|+2} \quad (|\gamma|\le K), $$ because $\sigma$ is bilinear, $\partial_\lambda\sigma$ is linear in $\mu$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Thus the absolute integrand is bounded by a finite sum of $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma\widehat a(\lambda)|\,\langle\lambda\rangle^{K+2}\, |\widehat b(\mu)|\,\langle\mu\rangle^{2K+2}. $$ For completeness, in Fourier dimension $n=2d$, if $2k>L+n$, then $$ \int\langle\lambda\rangle^L|\partial^\gamma\widehat f(\lambda)|\,d\lambda \le C\sum_{|\delta|\le2k}\|\partial^\delta(z^\gamma f)\|_{L^1} \le C p_M(f) $$ whenever $M\ge2k$ and $M>|\gamma|+n$: apply $(1-\Delta_z)^k$ to $z^\gamma f$, use its Fourier multiplier $\langle\lambda\rangle^{2k}$, and integrate the resulting $\langle z\rangle^{-M+|\gamma|}$ bound.
