support.exact_paragraph: The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,x-y)$ is an invertible linear map with absolute determinant $1$. The product of $a$, $u$, and $\overline u$ in the Weyl pairing is Schwartz in the transformed variables, so it is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5] and change of variables [F8] give $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)u(q-r/2)\overline{u(q+r/2)}\,dq\,dr\,d\xi . $$ Applying [F8] to the reflection $y=-r$ turns the last two factors and the exponential into the defining integrand of $W_\epsilon[u]$; hence the pairing identity follows. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

The function $g(x,y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz on $\mathbb R^{2d}$, because $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ is invertible linear and products of Schwartz functions are Schwartz. Its full negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform $\widehat g(\eta,\zeta)$ is Schwartz by [F3]; applying inverse Fourier transformation in $\eta$ by [F4] gives the partial transform $\int e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\zeta}g(x,y)\,dy$, Schwartz jointly in $(x,\zeta)$. The desired partial transform with phase $e^{-iy\cdot\zeta'}$ is this function at $\zeta=\zeta'/(2\pi)$; frequency dilation preserves Schwartz space. Replacing $\zeta'$ by $\xi/\epsilon$ and multiplying by $(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}$ therefore gives $W_\epsilon[u]\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})\subset L^1$. Conjugating the defining integral and applying [F8] to the reflection $y\mapsto-y$ returns the same integral, so $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

Fix $x$ and set $f_x(y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$. The integrand $\widehat f_x$ is Schwartz and hence in $L^1$. Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $\eta\mapsto\xi=\epsilon\eta$, whose Jacobian is $\epsilon^d$, to obtain the substitution $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$ and $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$. Write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$, also covered by [F8]. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

For the momentum marginal, $u\in\mathcal S\subseteq L^1$, so the double integral in $x,y$ is absolutely integrable by Fubini [F5]. The affine change $(x,y)\mapsto(q,r)=(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ has absolute determinant $1$ and $q-r=y$; [F8] therefore gives $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{-i(q-r)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(q)\overline{u(r)}\,dq\,dr=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$ The last equality is the product of the scaled Fourier integral with its complex conjugate. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

To see that nonnegativity fails, set $v_\epsilon(x)=\sqrt{2/\epsilon}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4}x e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. Substituting $x=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ and applying [F6] at Gaussian parameter $1/4$ gives $\int e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi$; one integration by parts [F7] then gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi/2$, hence $\int x^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon}dx=\sqrt\pi\,\epsilon^{3/2}/2$ and $\|v_\epsilon\|_2=1$. At the origin, $$ W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon](0,0)=-(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}\frac{1}{2\epsilon\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}}\int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}\,dy=-\frac1{\pi\epsilon}<0. $$ Here the Gaussian second moment is obtained from [F6] at $\xi=0$ by one integration by parts [F7]. Thus $W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon]$ is a normalized Schwartz Wigner distribution with a negative value. [given, A1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

support.exact_paragraph: The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,x-y)$ is an invertible linear map with absolute determinant $1$. The product of $a$, $u$, and $\overline u$ in the Weyl pairing is Schwartz in the transformed variables, so it is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5] and change of variables [F8] give $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)u(q-r/2)\overline{u(q+r/2)}\,dq\,dr\,d\xi . $$ Applying [F8] to the reflection $y=-r$ turns the last two factors and the exponential into the defining integrand of $W_\epsilon[u]$; hence the pairing identity follows. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

The function $g(x,y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz on $\mathbb R^{2d}$, because $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ is invertible linear and products of Schwartz functions are Schwartz. Its full negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform $\widehat g(\eta,\zeta)$ is Schwartz by [F3]; applying inverse Fourier transformation in $\eta$ by [F4] gives the partial transform $\int e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\zeta}g(x,y)\,dy$, Schwartz jointly in $(x,\zeta)$. The desired partial transform with phase $e^{-iy\cdot\zeta'}$ is this function at $\zeta=\zeta'/(2\pi)$; frequency dilation preserves Schwartz space. Replacing $\zeta'$ by $\xi/\epsilon$ and multiplying by $(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}$ therefore gives $W_\epsilon[u]\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})\subset L^1$. Conjugating the defining integral and applying [F8] to the reflection $y\mapsto-y$ returns the same integral, so $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

Fix $x$ and set $f_x(y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$. The integrand $\widehat f_x$ is Schwartz and hence in $L^1$. Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $\eta\mapsto\xi=\epsilon\eta$, whose Jacobian is $\epsilon^d$, to obtain the substitution $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$ and $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$. Write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$, also covered by [F8]. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

For the momentum marginal, $u\in\mathcal S\subseteq L^1$, so the double integral in $x,y$ is absolutely integrable by Fubini [F5]. The affine change $(x,y)\mapsto(q,r)=(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ has absolute determinant $1$ and $q-r=y$; [F8] therefore gives $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{-i(q-r)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(q)\overline{u(r)}\,dq\,dr=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$ The last equality is the product of the scaled Fourier integral with its complex conjugate. [given, A1, F2, F5, F8, algebra]

To see that nonnegativity fails, set $v_\epsilon(x)=\sqrt{2/\epsilon}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4}x e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. Substituting $x=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ and applying [F6] at Gaussian parameter $1/4$ gives $\int e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi$; one integration by parts [F7] then gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi/2$, hence $\int x^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon}dx=\sqrt\pi\,\epsilon^{3/2}/2$ and $\|v_\epsilon\|_2=1$. At the origin, $$ W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon](0,0)=-(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}\frac{1}{2\epsilon\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}}\int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}\,dy=-\frac1{\pi\epsilon}<0. $$ Here the Gaussian second moment is obtained from [F6] at $\xi=0$ by one integration by parts [F7]. Thus $W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon]$ is a normalized Schwartz Wigner distribution with a negative value. [given, A1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

1.1 By [F1], the input is a positive trace-one endomorphism on its finite tensor product. Apply [F5] to each bipartite grouping of a finite multipartite density operator; this makes every one-factor and two-factor marginal used in the Definition a density operator. Repeated partial traces use [F4] for the second factor and [F6] for the first factor, retaining the stated residual tensor-factor order. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 Each such density operator has finitely many eigenvalues in $[0,1]$, so the finite entropy sum in [F2] is a real number, including when some eigenvalues vanish. The relative entropy clause is defined on exactly the two support cases in [F3]. Therefore $I(A:B)$ and $I(A:C\mid B)$ are finite real-valued functions on the stated density operators, and $D$ has the extended-real domain specified in the Definition. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Fix integers $d,D\ge1$ and a translation invariant tensor $A^1,\ldots,A^d\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ with transfer map $\mathcal E(X):=\sum_iA^iXA^{i*}$. A matrix is positive semidefinite when it is Hermitian with nonnegative quadratic form on every vector. Let $\rho,\ell\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ be positive semidefinite matrices satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1,\qquad \mathcal E(\rho)=\rho,\qquad \mathcal E^*(\ell)=\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\ell\rho)=1,$$

where $\mathcal E^*(Y):=\sum_iA^{i*}YA^i$, equivalently the trace-pairing adjoint determined by $\operatorname{tr}(Y\mathcal E(X))=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal E^*(Y)X)$. For a contiguous block of $k\ge1$ sites, write $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and $J=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ for physical multi-indices, let $e_I$ be its ordered standard product basis, put $O_{I,J}:=\langle Oe_J,e_I\rangle$ for $O\in M_{d^k}(\mathbb C)$, and set $A^I:=A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_k}$. Define the transfer insertion map and local expectation by

$$\mathcal E_O(X):=\sum_{I,J}O_{I,J}A^JX(A^I)^*,\qquad \omega_k(O):=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_O(\rho)).$$

For any finite nonempty $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z$ and local observable $O\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, embed $O$ into the interval $[\min\Lambda,\max\Lambda]$ by inserting identities at missing sites and evaluate the same formula. For the empty region set $\omega_\varnothing(cI):=c$. These definitions give compatible positive normalized local functionals. Their unique density matrices $\rho_\Lambda$ obey $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$ whenever $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$. Assume Countable Choice. The transfer-generated infinite-chain state is the unique infinite algebraic state $\omega$ on the norm-completed quasi-local spin algebra whose restriction to every finite region is the defined local functional. No infinite tensor-product Hilbert space is selected.

For observables $O_A\in M_{d^a}(\mathbb C)$ and $O_B\in M_{d^b}(\mathbb C)$ on two fixed consecutive blocks, with $g\ge0$ identity sites between the blocks, the connected correlation is

$$\omega(O_A\otimes I^{\otimes g}\otimes O_B)-\omega(O_A)\omega(O_B).$$

1.1 The finite coefficient sum defining $\mathcal E_O(X)$ is complex-linear in both $O$ and $X$. For $O\ge0$, write its spectral decomposition as $O=\sum_\alpha|v_\alpha\rangle\langle v_\alpha|$, absorbing the square roots of the nonnegative eigenvalues into $v_\alpha$, and put $v_{\alpha,I}=\langle v_\alpha,e_I\rangle$. Then $O_{I,J}=\sum_\alpha v_{\alpha,I}\overline{v_{\alpha,J}}$, so with $K_\alpha:=\sum_J\overline{v_{\alpha,J}}A^J$ the insertion map satisfies $\mathcal E_O(X)=\sum_\alpha K_\alpha X K_\alpha^*\ge0$ whenever $X\ge0$. Diagonalizing $\ell$ by [F7] and expanding $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_O(\rho))$ as a weighted sum of nonnegative diagonal expectations shows $\omega_k(O)\ge0$. For $O=I_{d^k}$, $O_{I,J}=1$ if $I=J$ and $0$ otherwise, so the insertion sums over all length-$k$ words and equals $\mathcal E^k$. The fixed-point equations and $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\rho)=1$ give $\omega_k(I)=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E^k(\rho))=1$. Thus each contiguous-block functional is positive and normalized. [given, F1, F7, algebra]

2.1 Tensor-factor order in the definition gives $\mathcal E_{O\otimes P}=\mathcal E_O\circ\mathcal E_P$ for consecutive blocks: expanding both sides gives the same ordered product $A^{J_O}A^{J_P}X(A^{I_P})^*(A^{I_O})^*$. Inserting an identity site on the right composes with $\mathcal E$ on the input, which leaves $\rho$ fixed; inserting one on the left composes with $\mathcal E$ on the output, which leaves the trace pairing with $\ell$ fixed. Repeating these identities shows that the value is independent of the chosen containing interval and that restrictions to nested finite regions agree. A positive observable remains positive when identity factors are inserted, so the local functionals on arbitrary finite regions are positive and normalized as well. The empty-region convention is consistent because every local functional assigns one to the identity. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2]–[F4] each local positive normalized functional has a unique trace-one density $\rho_\Lambda$. For nested regions, step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}_{\Lambda'}((O\otimes I)\rho_{\Lambda'})=\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\rho_\Lambda)$ for every $O\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$. Applying the defining partial-trace pairing [F5] shows $\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'}))=\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\rho_\Lambda)$ for all $O$. Taking $O$ to be each matrix unit makes every matrix entry of the two matrices equal, so the density family is consistent. [given, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F6] to the consistent finite-region density family from step 3.1. Its hypotheses hold by [A1], [F2], [F3], and the positive trace-one property just proved. It yields a unique infinite algebraic state on the specified quasi-local algebra, with exactly these local restrictions and no chosen global Hilbert-space representation. This establishes that the transfer contractions in the Definition are well defined. [given, A1, F2, F3, F6, step 3.1] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the product inner product linear in its first argument. At each factor use
$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
For $1\le j\le N$, $X_j,Y_j,Z_j$ denote these matrices on factor $j$ and $I_2$ on every other factor. For real $h,J$ measured in joules define the finite open-chain matrix
$$H_N(h,J)=-h\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}X_jX_{j+1}.$$
The upper limit $N-1$ is the open-boundary convention: no term couples site $N$ to site $1$. Put $S_0=I_{\mathcal H_N}$ and $S_{j-1}=Z_1\cdots Z_{j-1}$ for $j>1$. The ordered Majorana operators are
$$\gamma_{2j-1}=S_{j-1}X_j,\qquad \gamma_{2j}=S_{j-1}Y_j\qquad(1\le j\le N).$$

1.1 Each displayed Pauli matrix is an everywhere-defined endomorphism of $\mathbb C^2$. Its tensor embedding $X_j,Y_j,Z_j$ is therefore an everywhere-defined endomorphism of the finite-dimensional product space $\mathcal H_N$, using the fixed factor order in [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Every $S_{j-1}$ and $\gamma_a$ is a finite product of such endomorphisms, and both sums defining $H_N$ are finite (the second is empty when $N=1$). Thus all displayed operators are well-defined matrices on $\mathcal H_N$; the only bond terms are exactly those indexed by $j<N$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Let $H_A=H_B=\mathbb C^2$ with the fixed orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ on each factor. Define the Bell density

$$\rho_\Phi=|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|,\qquad |\Phi\rangle=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2,$$

and the computational-basis-dephased density

$$\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}=\tfrac12|00\rangle\langle00|+\tfrac12|11\rangle\langle11|.$$

Both have marginals $I_2/2$, but their dimensionless mutual informations differ: $I(A:B)_{\rho_\Phi}=2\log2$ and $I(A:B)_{\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}}=\log2$. The displayed formula defines the dephased state; no measurement or experimental outcome is asserted.

1.1 The vector $|\Phi\rangle$ has norm one because $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$ are orthonormal, so $\rho_\Phi$ is a rank-one projection with trace one. The two orthogonal basis projections defining $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ are positive and each has trace one, so their half-weighted sum is also positive with trace one. Expanding $\rho_\Phi$ gives the four terms $\tfrac12|00\rangle\langle00|$, $\tfrac12|00\rangle\langle11|$, $\tfrac12|11\rangle\langle00|$, and $\tfrac12|11\rangle\langle11|$. In the partial trace over the second factor, the two off-diagonal terms vanish because the traced basis indices differ, by [F2]; in the trace over the first factor, the same is true by [F4]. In both cases the diagonal terms each contribute one half of the corresponding basis projection, so both marginals are $I_2/2$. Applying the same two formulas to $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ gives these marginals directly; they are density operators by [F3]. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The eigenvalues of $\rho_\Phi$ are $1,0,0,0$, those of $\rho_{\mathrm{diag}}$ are $1/2,1/2,0,0$, and those of each marginal are $1/2,1/2$. Substitution into [F1] yields $S(\rho_\Phi)=0$, $S(\rho_{\mathrm{diag}})=\log2$, and $S(I_2/2)=\log2$. Therefore the mutual informations are $2\log2$ and $\log2$, respectively, as stated. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section: Assume Countable Choice. Use the standard inner product on $\mathbb C^2$ and its ordered basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$. For $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, let $E_{ij}\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ have entry $1$ in row $i$, column $j$, and entry $0$ elsewhere, with rows and columns ordered $0,1$. For each integer $N\ge2$, index the factors cyclically modulo $N$ and let $A^0=|0\rangle\langle0|=E_{00}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^1=|1\rangle\langle1|=E_{11}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The periodic trace contraction has amplitude $\operatorname{tr}(A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_N})$ on basis vector $|i_1\cdots i_N\rangle$ and equals $|0^N\rangle+|1^N\rangle$; after normalization it is the GHZ vector $(|0^N\rangle+|1^N\rangle)/\sqrt2$. The transfer map fixes $E_{00}$ and $E_{11}$ and annihilates $E_{01}$ and $E_{10}$. With $\rho=I_2/2$ and $\ell=I_2$, the associated infinite transfer state has $\omega(Z_1)=0$ and $\omega(Z_1I^{\otimes g}Z_{g+2})=1$ for every integer gap $g\ge0$, where $Z=|0\rangle\langle0|-|1\rangle\langle1|$ acts on one site. Thus its connected $Z$ correlation is exactly $1$ at every gap and does not decay.

1.1 Each $A^i$ is the diagonal projection $E_{ii}$. A product $A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_N}$ is zero if the word contains both $0$ and $1$, and is $E_{00}$ or $E_{11}$ for the two constant words. Its trace is therefore one exactly for those two words and zero otherwise, proving the unnormalized periodic vector formula. The two basis vectors $|0^N\rangle$ and $|1^N\rangle$ are orthonormal, so its squared norm is $2$ and the stated normalization follows. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 On the basis $\{E_{ij}:i,j\in\{0,1\}\}$ defined in the Statement, $\mathcal E(E_{00})=E_{00}$, $\mathcal E(E_{11})=E_{11}$, and $\mathcal E(E_{01})=\mathcal E(E_{10})=0$. Thus the fixed subspace $\{X\in M_2(\mathbb C):\mathcal E(X)=X\}$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{E_{00},E_{11}\}$ and has dimension two. Also $\mathcal E(\rho)=\rho$, $\mathcal E^*(\ell)=\ell$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\rho)=1$, so [F2] applies under [A1]. The insertion for $Z$ is $\mathcal E_Z(X)=A^0XA^{0*}-A^1XA^{1*}$, whence $\mathcal E_Z(\rho)=(E_{00}-E_{11})/2$, $\mathcal E^g\mathcal E_Z(\rho)=\mathcal E_Z(\rho)$, and $\mathcal E_Z\mathcal E^g\mathcal E_Z(\rho)=I_2/2$. Therefore $\omega(Z_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_Z(\rho))=0$ and $\omega(Z_1I^{\otimes g}Z_{g+2})=\operatorname{tr}(\ell I_2/2)=1$ for every $g\ge0$. Subtracting the product of the one-point expectations gives connected correlation $1$. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix $C^*$-identity for the local spin algebras. Let $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, be a $C^1$ finite-range interaction path on $\mathbb Z^d$, with uniform range, support-cardinality, weighted interaction norm, and weighted derivative norm as in the interaction definition. Assume the selected finite-volume bands along a fixed increasing exhaustion $\Lambda_n\uparrow\mathbb Z^d$ are locally fixed spectral clusters with uniform gap $\gamma>0$. Let

$$D_{\Lambda_n}(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)\, \tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}\!\left(H'_{\Lambda_n}(s)\right)\,dt,$$

where energies are dimensionless ($\hbar=1$) and $W_\gamma$ and the filtered derivative are as in the finite-volume spectral-generator lemma. For every $\rho>d$, there are self-adjoint local interactions $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, supported in $Z\subseteq\Lambda_n$, such that

$$D_{\Lambda_n}(s)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda_n}\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s),\qquad \sup_n\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(s)\|_{F_\rho}<\infty.$$

For every fixed finite nonempty $Z\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the coefficient $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, set to zero when $Z\not\subseteq\Lambda_n$, converges in norm uniformly in $s$ to a self-adjoint $\Psi_\infty(Z,s)$. The limiting interaction has finite $F_\rho$-norm for every $\rho>d$.

For every finite $\Lambda_n$ and nonempty support $Z\subseteq\Lambda_n$, the coefficient $s\mapsto\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$ is norm-continuous.

1.1 For each finite nonempty $Y\subseteq\Lambda_n$, set $B_{Y,n}(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)\, \tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(\Phi'_s(Y))\,dt.$ For fixed $n,Y,t$, the finite matrix integrand is continuous in $s$, and it is bounded by $\sup_s\|\Phi'_s(Y)\||W_\gamma(t)|$, an integrable majorant. Dominated convergence makes $B_{Y,n}(s)$ norm-continuous. Linearity of the finite sum and [F2] give $D_{\Lambda_n}(s)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Y\subseteq\Lambda_n}B_{Y,n}(s)$. Define $Y_k=\{x:d_\infty(x,Y)\le k\}$, $E_{Y_k}^{(n)}:=E_{Y_k\cap\Lambda_n}$, and shells $\Delta^0_{Y,n}=E_{Y_0}^{(n)}(B_{Y,n}),\qquad \Delta^k_{Y,n}=E_{Y_k}^{(n)}(B_{Y,n})-E_{Y_{k-1}}^{(n)}(B_{Y,n})\quad(k\ge1).$ For all sufficiently large $k$, $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n=\Lambda_n$, so the sum of these shells is $B_{Y,n}$. Each shell is self-adjoint and supported in $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n$. Grouping the finitely many shells by this support defines $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$ and proves the displayed decomposition. Each expectation is a fixed linear map, so the shell and grouped coefficients are norm-continuous in $s$. [given, A1, F2, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 Let $a>0$ be the weight parameter and $v=2C_{F_a}\sup_s\|\Phi_s\|_{F_a}$, with $V=1+v$. For $z\in\Lambda_n\setminus Y_k$, the supports $Y$ and $\{z\}$ are disjoint; [F3] and the local-expectation estimate [F4] give $\left\|\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(\Phi'_s(Y)) -E_{Y_k}^{(n)}\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(\Phi'_s(Y))\right\| \le C|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|e^{v|t|}e^{-ak/2},$ where the lattice shell count and the exponential factor in $F_a$ give one constant $C$ independent of $Y,n,s,t$. The same difference is at most $2\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$ by contractivity. Split the filtered integral at $T_k=ak/(4V)$. On $|t|\le T_k$ the first bound is at most $C|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|e^{-ak/4}$; on $|t|>T_k$, the Schwartz-tail construction in [F2] gives $\int_{|t|>T_k}|W_\gamma(t)|dt\le C_N(1+k)^{-N}$ for each $N$. Since $\Delta^k_{Y,n}$ is a difference of the (k)- and $(k-1)$-expectations, its norm is bounded by the sum of these two expectation errors. Thus, after increasing $C_N$, for every $N$ there is a constant $C_N$ independent of $Y,n,s,k$ such that $\|\Delta^k_{Y,n}(s)\|\le C_N|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|(1+k)^{-N}.$ For $k=0$, the same estimate with an enlarged $C_N$ follows from $\|E_Y(B_{Y,n})\|\le\|W_\gamma\|_1\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The finite-range path has a uniform range $R$, so $x,y\in Y_k$ implies $d_\infty(x,y)\le R+2k$. Also [F1] at $x=y$ gives $\sup_s\sum_{Y\ni x}|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|<\infty$. Since $x\in Y_k$ forces $Y\cap B_k(x)\ne\varnothing$, the sum of $|Y|\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|$ over such $Y$ is at most $C(k+1)^d$. For each fixed $s$, summing the shell estimate from step 2.1 over all $Y,k$ with $x,y\in Y_k$ gives $\sum_{\substack{Z\subseteq\Lambda_n\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)\| \le C_N\sum_{k\ge (d_\infty(x,y)-R)/2}(1+k)^{d-N}.$ For any prescribed $\rho>d$, choose $N>\rho+d+1$; the last tail is bounded by $C_\rho(1+d_\infty(x,y))^{-\rho}$. The bound is independent of $s$ and $n$, so taking their suprema outside the support sum proves the stated uniform $F_\rho$-norm bound. No sum of separate time suprema is asserted; all finite-volume sums are finite and their nonnegative shell bounds are dominated by the displayed convergent scalar series. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix a finite support $Z$. Once $\Lambda_n$ contains the $(2\operatorname{diam}Z+1)$-neighborhood of $Z$, any shell with support $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n=Z$ has $Y\subseteq Z$ and $k\le\operatorname{diam}Z$; otherwise $Y_k\cap\Lambda_n$ would contain a point in that neighborhood outside $Z$. Thus only finitely many pairs $(Y,k)$ contribute to $\Psi_{\Lambda_n}(Z,s)$, and their shell projections are the fixed $E_{Y_k}$ once $n$ is large. By [A1], [F6], and [F5], for each fixed $s$, $\tau_t^{\Lambda_n,\Phi_s}(A)$ converges locally uniformly on compact $t$-intervals. The same boundary estimate in the proof of [F5] is uniform in $s$, because the path has uniform finite range and interaction bounds. For $A=\Phi'_s(Y)$, uniformity over $s$ follows by covering the compact finite-dimensional set $\{\Phi'_s(Y):s\in[0,1]\}$ by a finite norm net and using contractivity of the dynamics. The tails $|t|>T$ are bounded uniformly by $2\sup_s\|\Phi'_s(Y)\|\int_{|t|>T}|W_\gamma(t)|dt$, which tends to zero by [F2]. Hence every contributing filtered term converges uniformly in $s$, defining $\Psi_\infty(Z,s)$. The $F_\rho$-norm bound passes to the limit by taking the limit on each finite set of support terms and then the supremum. [given, A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $H_\Lambda(s)$ be the finite-volume self-adjoint matrix of a $C^1$ interaction path on the dimensionless parameter $s\in[0,1]$, and let the selected spectral band be a locally fixed spectral cluster, separated from its complement by $\gamma>0$ uniformly in $s$, in the sense of the interaction definition. Choose a positive reference energy $E_0$ and measure physical energies in units of $E_0$; $H_\Lambda$, $H'_\Lambda$, and $\gamma$ in this statement are dimensionless, and the Fourier evolution uses $\hbar=1$. Let $P_\Lambda(s)$ be the orthogonal spectral projection onto that band. Then $P_\Lambda$ is $C^1$. There is a real, odd, integrable function $W_\gamma\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, with Fourier convention

$$\widehat W_\gamma(\omega):=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)e^{it\omega}\,dt,$$

such that $\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)=i/\omega$ whenever $|\omega|\ge\gamma$, and for every integer $N\ge0$ there is $c_N<\infty$ with

$$\int_{|t|>T}|W_\gamma(t)|\,dt\le c_N(1+T)^{-N}\qquad(T\ge0).$$

The finite matrix

$$D_\Lambda(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}W_\gamma(t)e^{itH_\Lambda(s)} H_\Lambda'(s)e^{-itH_\Lambda(s)}\,dt$$

is self-adjoint and satisfies

$$P_\Lambda'(s)=i[D_\Lambda(s),P_\Lambda(s)].$$

1.1 Define $\chi(\omega)=e\exp(-1/(1-(\omega/\gamma)^2))$ for $|\omega|<\gamma$, and $\chi(\omega)=0$ otherwise. The exponential tends to zero faster than every power at the endpoints, so $\chi$ is real, even, smooth, compactly supported in $[-\gamma,\gamma]$, and $\chi(0)=1$. Define $w(t)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int\chi(\omega)e^{-it\omega}\,d\omega$. By [A1], [F3], and the sign/scale conversion stated in [F3], $w$ is Schwartz, real and even, its Fourier transform $\widehat w(\omega)=\int w(t)e^{it\omega}dt$ equals $\chi(\omega)$, and $\int w=1$. For $t>0$ put $W_\gamma(t)=\int_t^\infty w(v)\,dv$; for $t<0$ put $W_\gamma(t)=-\int_{-\infty}^t w(v)\,dv$; set $W_\gamma(0)=0$. Evenness and unit integral make $W_\gamma$ odd with one-sided limits $W_\gamma(0^\pm)=\pm\frac12$. For every $N$, a Schwartz bound $|w(v)|\le c(1+|v|)^{-N-2}$ on either tail gives $|W_\gamma(t)|\le c'(1+|t|)^{-N-1}$; hence $W_\gamma\in L^1$ and has the stated tail estimate. Integration by parts on the two half-lines, accounting for the jump of size $1$ at zero and using $W_\gamma'=-w$ away from zero, gives $-\widehat w(\omega)=-1-i\omega\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)$. Thus $\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)=i(1-\chi(\omega))/\omega$ for $\omega\ne0$, so it equals $i/\omega$ for $|\omega|\ge\gamma$. [given, A1, F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Fix $s_0$. By the locally fixed spectral-cluster hypothesis and [F2], choose a finite union of positively oriented contours $\Gamma$ surrounding exactly the selected eigenvalues and staying a positive distance from the remaining spectrum, with the same selected eigenvalues enclosed for nearby $s$. For $s$ near $s_0$, $\|H_\Lambda(s)-H_\Lambda(s_0)\|$ is small; factoring $zI-H_\Lambda(s)$ through $zI-H_\Lambda(s_0)$ and using the norm-convergent Neumann series keeps every $z\in\Gamma$ in the resolvent set. The contour projection $P_\Lambda(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-H_\Lambda(s))^{-1}\,dz$ is therefore $C^1$, since the inverse matrix is $C^1$ in $s$. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H_\Lambda(s)$, write its eigenvalues as $E_m$ and the band indicator as $p_m\in\{0,1\}$. Differentiating $P^2=P$ gives $P'_{mn}=0$ when $p_m=p_n$. Differentiating $HP=PH$ gives $P'_{mn}=(p_m-p_n)H'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)$ when $p_m\ne p_n$; the denominator has magnitude at least $\gamma$. The integral defining $D_\Lambda$ converges in norm because $W_\gamma\in L^1$; it is self-adjoint because $W_\gamma$ is real and each conjugated $H_\Lambda'$ is self-adjoint. Dominated convergence, using continuity and boundedness of $H_\Lambda'(s)$ on the compact interval and the integrable majorant $2\sup_s\|H_\Lambda'(s)\||W_\gamma(t)|$, shows $D_\Lambda(s)$ is norm-continuous. Its matrix entries are $(D_\Lambda)_{mn}=H'_{mn}\widehat W_\gamma(E_m-E_n)=iH'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)$ across the band gap. Hence $i[D_\Lambda,P_\Lambda]_{mn}=(p_n-p_m)i(D_\Lambda)_{mn}=(p_m-p_n)H'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)=P'_{mn}$ across the gap, and both sides vanish within either band block. This proves the identity in every matrix entry. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
Let $d\ge1$, $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, and $d_\infty$ be the max-coordinate metric. For $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$, $F_a(r)=e^{-ar}F(r)$ with $a>0$, and $F_\rho(r)=(1+r)^{-\rho}$ with $\rho>d$, each weight $G\in\{F,F_a,F_\rho\}$ is summable on $\Gamma$. Its convolution constant

$$C_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y))} {G(d_\infty(x,y))},$$

where $C_F$ uses this same formula with the base weight $F=F_{d+1}$. Each such constant is finite and positive. In particular, for all $x,y\in\Gamma$,

$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}G(d_\infty(x,z))G(d_\infty(z,y)) \le C_G\,G(d_\infty(x,y)).$$

The constant $C_{F_a}$ may be taken to be the convolution constant $C_F$ of $F$, independently of $a$.

1.1 For $k\ge1$, the $d_\infty$-shell of radius $k$ has $(2k+1)^d-(2k-1)^d\le c_d(k+1)^{d-1}$ sites, by factoring the difference of powers; the radius-zero shell has one site. Therefore $\sum_z F_\rho(d_\infty(x,z))\le c_d\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)^{d-1-\rho}<\infty$, and $\sum_zF_a(d_\infty(x,z))\le\sum_zF(d_\infty(x,z))<\infty$. The bounds are independent of $x$ by translation invariance. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Write $r=d_\infty(x,y)$. For $G=F_\rho$, the triangle inequality places every $z$ in at least one of the sets $d_\infty(x,z)\ge r/2$ or $d_\infty(z,y)\ge r/2$. On the first set, $G(d_\infty(x,z))\le2^\rho G(r)$; summing the other factor over all $z$ is bounded by the finite shell sum in step 1.1. The second set gives the same bound with $x,y$ exchanged. Hence $C_{F_\rho}\le2^{\rho+1}\sum_zF_\rho(d_\infty(0,z))<\infty$. For $F_a$, the triangle inequality gives $e^{-a(d(x,z)+d(z,y))}\le e^{-ar}$; the same splitting argument applied to $F=F_{d+1}$, for which $d+1>d$, yields $C_F<\infty$, and then $\sum_zF_a(d(x,z))F_a(d(z,y))\le C_FF_a(r)$. Positivity of each weight and the $z=x$ summand show $C_G>0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

supporting_paragraphs.exact_paragraph_or_section:
For every finite $X\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the map $E_X$ of the normalized-trace-expectation definition is a unital positive contraction on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and has a unique contractive extension $E_X:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A_X$. For $B\in\mathcal A_Y$, $Y$ finite,

$$\|B-E_X(B)\|\le \sum_{z\in Y\setminus X}\ \sup_{\substack{V\in\mathcal A_{\{z\}}\\V^*V=VV^*=I}} \|[B,V]\|.$$

1.1 On $\mathbb C^q$ in the standard basis $e_j$, $0\le j<q$, define $S e_j=e_{j+1\ {\rm mod}\ q}$ and $D e_j=e^{2\pi i j/q}e_j$. The $q^2$ unitaries $S^aD^b$, $0\le a,b<q$, satisfy $q^{-2}\sum_{a,b=0}^{q-1}(S^aD^b)^*R(S^aD^b) =q^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(R)I_q\qquad(R\in M_q(\mathbb C)).$ Indeed, averaging over $b$ cancels each off-diagonal matrix unit because its phase is a nontrivial $q$-th root sum, and averaging the surviving diagonal units over $a$ gives their arithmetic mean times $I_q$; for $q=1$ the formula is the identity. Applying this one-site twirl on each factor in $Y\setminus X$ yields the normalized partial trace of [F1]. Each twirl is an average of unitary conjugations, so it is unital, positive, and contractive. The formula is unchanged when an extra identity factor is added, since its normalized trace is $1$; hence $E_X$ is consistent on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Contractivity extends it uniquely to the completion, and its range remains in the closed finite-dimensional subalgebra $\mathcal A_X$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Enumerate $Y\setminus X=\{z_1,\ldots,z_k\}$ and write $E_{z_j}$ for the one-site twirl. The commuting twirls satisfy $B-E_X(B)=\sum_{j=1}^k E_{z_1}\cdots E_{z_{j-1}}\bigl(B-E_{z_j}(B)\bigr).$ For any $C\in\mathcal A_Y$, the average formula gives $\|C-E_{z_j}(C)\|\le\sup_{V_z}\|C-V_z^*CV_z\|=\sup_{V_z}\|[C,V_z]\|$, where $V_z$ ranges over the one-site unitaries. Each preceding twirl is contractive and commutes with conjugation by $V_z$, so its term in the displayed sum is at most $\sup_{V_z}\|[B,V_z]\|$.
